articles.body:
John Healey tells MPs he is confident budget will be good for growth despite OBR not finding evidence to prove this

John Healey, the chancellor, is giving evidence to the Commons Treasury committee. When John Glen, a Conservative member of the committee and former Treasury minister, asked him if he was worried that the Office for Budget Responsibility said they could not identify any measures in the budget that would have a significant impact on growth, Healey did not accept this.

He said that Glen was right to say the OBR did not identify any measures that they wanted to include in their growth scorecard.

But he went on:

I’m not terribly worried about that because I believe in the months ahead, and the next year or two, the sort of measures [in the budget] on enterprise I believe, the measures on devolution I believe, the measures on energy and also on AI will start to feed through and we will see that impact on growth.

And in the end, yes, of course, the formal figures matter, the forecasts matter.

But, actually, it’s also business confidence [that matters].

The OBR normally only includes growth measures in their scorecard if they will increase growth by at least 0.1% of GDP.

As Graeme Wearden reports on his business live blog, Healey also told the committee he was “dismayed” by a leak to Bloomberg on the morning of the budget saying the new bank tax would be less onerous than the City assumed.

John Healey, the chancellor, has told MPs that he is confident the measures in his budget will be good for growth – even though the Office for Budget Responsibility did not make that assessment. (See 3.04pm.)

The government will struggle to deliver on “haphazard” NHS reforms set in motion by its predecessors, a new report has warned. As the Press Assocation reports,the health service is currently juggling “dozens” of priorities set by Keir Starmer and Wes Streeting, with the focus on waiting times, structural reorganisation and finances preventing the NHS “from making progress on other priorities”. The Institute for Government (IfG) and Nuffield Foundation urged Andy Burnham and Yvette Cooper to reduce the “fantasyland” 18-week waiting time target and clarify their own goals for the health service. Labour’s 2024 manifesto pledged to meet the standard of 92% of patients waiting less than 18 weeks for treatment by the end of parliament. However, the new report predicts this will be missed by a “wide margin”.

For a full list of all the stories covered on the blog today, do scroll through the list of key event headlines near the top of the blog.

Morgan McSweeney calls for rethink of UK cabinet ministers’ ‘quasi-judicial’ powers

Keir Starmer’s former chief of staff, Morgan McSweeney, has called for a rethink of “quasi-judicial” powers given to cabinet ministers such as the energy secretary’s ability to approve future oil and gas fields. Rowena Mason has the story.

The Restore Britain MP Rupert Lowe says he has tabled an early day motion saying that “the English, Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish are historic people with distinct ethnic identities”. This is a direct attempt to counter the argument being made by the Lib Dem MP Josh Babarinde, and supported at PMQs today by Andy Burnham (see 12.29pm), about how black English and Asian English should be recognised identities.

David Cameron claims Brexit not to blame for main economic problems facing UK, and doesn't back rejoining EU

David Cameron led the campaign to keep the UK in the EU in 2016. He resigned as PM after he lost. But he is not in favour of trying to rejoin.

In an interview with Bloomberg’s Mishal Husain, Cameron argued that Brexit was not to blame for the most serious economic problems facing Britain.

If you look at the economic problems we have today, I don’t really think they’ve got anything to do with Brexit at all. I mean, our economic problems are we are overspending, over-borrowing, over-taxing, over-regulated, and far too much being spent on working-age welfare. Those are a set of problems that have nothing to do with Brexit.

We need a government that actually gets spending under control, gets taxes down, helps entrepreneurs, deals with our borrowing problem, reforms the welfare, and massively deregulates so we can build houses, build infrastructure. None of those have got anything to do with Europe.

So that’s my point. Do we really want to go into another decade-long debate about whether we should be in or out, when actually we should deal with our own problems while making the partnership model work?

Cameron also argued that, if British politicians raised the prospect of rejoining one day, they were less likely to get a good partnership deal now.

If you start endlessly producing this idea that we’re actually on a path to rejoining, I think you’re in danger of getting a less good partnership deal because of course the EU countries will just think, ‘Well, these guys are gonna rejoin anyway, so what’s the point in giving them a good partnership deal?’

Healey says homeleness and VAWG could be priorities for new 'preventative DEL' protected spending status

Labour’s Seema Malhotra asked John Healey at the Treasury committee about his plans to ringfence spending on some programmes deemed preventative. She asked how much spending was likely to be included in this new PDEL (preventative departmental expenditure limits) category, and how departments would decide what counted as PDEL.

Healey replied:

The short answer is that it’s premature to be able to give you that sort of detail …

The thinking behind this is really twofold.

One is that we recognise in CDEL [capital DEL] the particular value and importance of long-term investment. And this is a way of recognising the potential long-term value of preventative spending …

The second thing is that it is a recognition that in some of the most complex and intractable social service delivery [areas] – and arguably economic [areas] – [there is] the complexity of having multiple departments with different budget lines that may or may not make a contribution.

I would expect a limited number of areas to try and demonstrate in practice a different way, not just of accounting and allocating budgets, but managing most effectively our ability to tackle some deep-seated problems.

Obvious, potential priorities might be rough sleeping, homelessness, violence against women and girls, where short-term decisions often load extra costs in other parts of the system.

This is a way for government to get beyond some of those sort of barriers.

Treasury permanent secretary backs Healey in saying Truss's mini-budget to blame for UK's above-average borrowing costs

At the Treasury committee, the Labour MP Andrew Lewin asked John Healey why UK government borrowing costs (or gilt yields) were higher than for comparable countries, even though the debt-to-GDP ratio is lower than in countries like France and Italy.

Healey replied:

I don’t really want to labour it, but quite honestly our gilt yields were pretty much in step with European countries until the Liz Truss mini-budget. We’ve been paying a premium since then …

I think if you look at the upheaval in the bond markets in recent weeks, you’ll have seen that Britain can’t avoid the storm. But we don’t happen to be at the centre of the storm in the way that we have potentially been in the past. That has been difficult for France. And you’ve seen the relative rise in yields for France in that period of turmoil and uncertainty have outstripped the UK.

At that point Healey invited James Bowler, the permanent secretary at the Treasury who was giving evidence with him, to comment. Bowler told the committee:

The chancellor is absolutely right about when we diverged from the G7 average …

I think it’s probably worth saying that throughout this Middle East conflict, the UK has been very much in line with the G7 average and other countries which, frustratingly, have seen borrowing costs rise. And they’re rising predominantly because [the war] means more inflation, via energy, and tougher fiscal situations.

The Reform UK MS (member of the Senedd) Cai Parry-Jones has posted on social media a copy of the letter the Senedd llywydd (presiding officer), Huw Irranca-Davies, has sent to MSs asking them not to challenge his Joe Martin ruling on social media. Parry-Jones says it is a “dystopian” attempt to silence people.

Reform UK Senedd members abandon press briefing when challenged over racism claims

In Cardiff some Reform UK Senedd members have held a press conference about their decision to boycott this afternoon’s plenary session. (See 2.41pm.) In a post and video clip on social media, Will Hayward describes it as one of the most bizarre press conferences he has attended as a journalist.

Reform UK held a press conference and said they would not be carry out their jobs of sitting the Senedd today to defend the “free speech” of Joe Martin MS.

In that same press conference Mr Martin snapped “how dare you ask that question” after a WalesOnline journalist asked if the party was racist.

When challenged about this they walked away.

In response, Liz Saville Roberts, the Plaid Cymru leader at Westminster, has posted these on social media.

Running scared of free speech.

Reform drop any pretence of representing constituents as a serious opposition party with today’s ‘don’t you dare hold us to account’ boycott.

Reform are boycotting their own debate on remembrance and veterans on Armistice Day.

Nothing says ‘standing up for veterans’ quite like not bothering to turn up for them.

Healey tells MPs government 'is behind third runway at Heathrow' - despite Burnham recently equivocating on issue

Healey told the Treasury committee that support for a third runway at Heathrow is government policy.

In response to a question from Labour’s Siobhain McDonagh, who asked about the third runway, Healey said:

The government is behind a third runway at Heathrow, and I’m part of the government.

Interestingly, that is not the answer Andy Burnham gave when he was asked about this in an interview during Labour conference. Burnham, who is reportedly sceptical about the case for a third runway, said this was a “contested issued” and mainly a matter for Labour MPs. He also claimed it would not be appropriate to comment because a consultation was underway.

McDonagh, a London MP and a supporter of a third runway, said told Healey she was frustrated how long it was taking.

UPDATE:Healey said:

Our experience in recent decades, is it not, is that successful airports are very often an engine for economic growth in the wider area? That’s as true in Manchester as it is true in parts of London and elsewhere.

In terms of the assessment following the consultation period, that’s not led by the Treasury. That’s led by the Department for Transport, and the government is working through the responses and the further update information we’ve got from that.

Healey dismisses IFS criticism of new founder's relief tax cut, saying views of those 'in the field' count more

At the committee, Healey was also asked about a comment from Helen Miller, head of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, criticising one of the measures in his budget, the founder’s relief tax cut for entrepreneurs. She said it was “bonkers”.

Healey said he had a lot of respect for Miller. “But, to be quite honest, I look more to those who are in the field,” he said.

He said the founder’s relief policy had been warmly welcomed by the Startup Coalition, which represents tech startups.

John Healey tells MPs he is confident budget will be good for growth despite OBR not finding evidence to prove this

John Healey, the chancellor, is giving evidence to the Commons Treasury committee. When John Glen, a Conservative member of the committee and former Treasury minister, asked him if he was worried that the Office for Budget Responsibility said they could not identify any measures in the budget that would have a significant impact on growth, Healey did not accept this.

He said that Glen was right to say the OBR did not identify any measures that they wanted to include in their growth scorecard.

But he went on:

I’m not terribly worried about that because I believe in the months ahead, and the next year or two, the sort of measures [in the budget] on enterprise I believe, the measures on devolution I believe, the measures on energy and also on AI will start to feed through and we will see that impact on growth.

And in the end, yes, of course, the formal figures matter, the forecasts matter.

But, actually, it’s also business confidence [that matters].

The OBR normally only includes growth measures in their scorecard if they will increase growth by at least 0.1% of GDP.

As Graeme Wearden reports on his business live blog, Healey also told the committee he was “dismayed” by a leak to Bloomberg on the morning of the budget saying the new bank tax would be less onerous than the City assumed.

Reform UK Senedd members boycott plenary session as protest about colleague facing speaking ban

Reform UK members of the Senedd are boycotting today’s plenary session as a protest against a member of their group being told he won’t be called to speak until he apologises for comments about immigrants that were deemed offensive. (See 11.04am.)

Explaining their move, Helen Jenner, the Reform UK leader in Wales, said:

The people of Wales gave Reform a clear mandate to raise their concerns and to be their voice.

It is now clear that the freedom of speech of one of our Senedd members is being curtailed, meaning his constituents are being silenced.

We stand behind Joe [Martin], and we will not attend today’s plenary session in protest at his treatment.

Every Reform MS will be in their Senedd office working hard for our constituents.

And Martin said in a statement:

My voters sent me to the Senedd to speak on their behalf.

I am being blocked from doing so, and now it’s clear that I have fewer rights than the people who elected me.

That cannot be the situation in a national parliament.

The Reform UK MSs (members of the Senedd) still intend to take part in any votes at the end of the session.

Reform UK's general secretary leaves, with Labour claiming he's 'fall guy' for scandals

Ben Quinn

Ben Quinn is a Guardian political correspondent.

Reform UK’s general secretary has left the role as Nigel Farage’s party continues to face turmoil over questions about vetting failures and professionalisation.

The departure of Tom Waterhouse comes after Reform UK’s leader on Hampshire county council, George Madgwick, was charged with 12 counts of rape and one of distributing indecent images of a child.

Waterhouse, an experienced public affairs executive who previously worked in the Westminster thinktank world and for the Crown Estate, had only been recruited in August last year. Labour described him as Reform’s “latest fall-guy” for problems at the party.

A Reform UK spokesman said:

Tom Waterhouse has left his role with Reform UK. The party leader has now appointed an interim general secretary.

However, his departure comes as a blow to Reform’s drive towards professionalisation, a project which he had been at the centre of.

He had been involved in a major recruitment push, bankrolled by wealthy donors, as well as the selection of its candidates for a future general election.

Waterhouse had also been involved with Adam Richardson, a long-standing associate of Farage, in the party’s internal investigation into two of its senior officials, James Orr and Dan Jukes, which cleared them of breaking laws that ban foreign donations, despite the matter remaining under police investigation.

However, the recent case of Madgwick severely embarrassed the party and once again brought the question of Reform’s candidate vetting process into the spotlight.

That process is now run by Paul Nuttall, the party’s deputy chair and former Ukip leader, but Waterhouse also reflects continuing organisational turmoil at Reform.

As the scandals pile up for Reform, everyone is being forced to take the blame except Nigel Farage. Their general secretary is the latest fall guy, but we all know nobody in Reform makes a decision without Farage’s approval.

Farage has recently not concealed his unhappiness at continued failures when it comes to vetting and other matters.

“I wasn’t very happy,” said the Reform UK leader when asked why Madgwick, who was arrested in January over multiple alleged sexual offences, was still in his role nearly 10 months later.

Farage last month also blamed “staff incompetence” for a poor turnout and a half-empty hall during a Reform UK economic policy launch event in London.

Staff at Reform’s Millbank HQ were informed on Wednesday that Waterhouse was leaving. He is one of a number of figures who had been seen as major assets to Reform’s push for power who have parted company or been sidelined in recent times.

They include Tim Montgomerie, a high-profile activist who defected from the Conservatives, who was suspended after he criticised Farage’s decision not to attend the count when he won the Clacton byelection.

Madgwick, who is scheduled to appear at Portsmouth magistrates court on 25 November, denies any wrongdoing.

No 10 defends Miliband over interview with Russell Brand in 2015

Downing Street has defended Ed Miliband amid questions over his past contact with Russell Brand, the Press Association reports.

At the post-PMQs lobby briefing, asked whether Miliband, who did a high-profile and controversial interview with Brand on Brand’s YouTube channel during the 2015 election campaign, should address his previous contact with the rapist comedian, the PM’s political spokesman said:

The prime minister was asked about this on Friday in an interview with the BBC. As he said, it’s not always the case that people know everything about people in public life, but what is important is where there is wrongdoing, it is exposed.

The PM also praised the bravery of the victims, saying credit to the victims, huge credit for the courage it’s taken, but also for the journalists that have exposed this.

The spokesperson also said the Miliband/Brand interview was “long time ago”.

Kemi Badenoch is on record as saying she treats PMQs like panto. It is not a ridiculous view; in many respects, it is all about theatre and performance, the jokes matter (often they are all that anyone remembers by the end of the afternoon), and Badenoch started impressing her MPs (and wider audiences) when she abandoned an overly-analytical approach to PMQs, and started playing it for laughs, or Punch and Judy-style aggro, instead.

If you subscribe to the Badenoch thesis, today was one of her best outings against Burnham. She was consistently funny and withering, and delivered an effective put-down about Ed Miliband too. Her MPs seemed to like it, and on Tory social media she is getting predictably good reviews. This matters a bit; it is better than a Tory leader getting bad reviews in the Tory media.

And there are moments when a well-crafted joke can deliver a win at PMQs. When William Hague was in the job Badenoch is doing now, that happened most weeks.

But to convey mastery at PMQs, rather than just making people laugh, the humour has to be linked to a wider argument, and today it wasn’t. At least, it wasn’t linked to a wider argument that was compelling. Badenoch’s main challenge was about the Rosebank oilfield, and the government’s failure (yet) to approve it. Burnham could acceptably see this off with a reference to it being subjudice. Beyond that, Badenoch was essentially just running an ‘admit you’re useless’ diatribe. With some PMs, in some circumstances, that’s enough. But Burnham is not anywhere close to that point yet and so Badenoch’s questions just sounded like knee-jerk negativity – albeit artfully done.

For an alternative (and better) theory of PMQs, do read this thread from Theo Bertram, a former Labour No 10 adviser (in the Blair/Brown years) who now runs a thinktank. This is his conclusion:

I worked on 119 PMQs in No10 and I would observe that winning individual PMQs (because you landed a blow or a joke) matters less than establishing an argument over a term (eg. He didn’t fix the roof while the sun was shining). That’s how you win at PMQs in the long run.

On jokes, Badenoch is winning. But, on most or all of the main arguments, Burnham still has the upper hand. And on personality too he also has an advantage because he sounds fair and reasonable, as he did again today, which isn’t always a virtue associated with the opposition leader.

articles.title: United States warns Madagascar over growing security ties with Russia
articles.summary: The deputy head of US Africa Command said similar partnerships with military-led governments in Africa have failed to improve security.
articles.preview: Madagascar The United States has warned Madagascar against strengthening its military ties with Russia. The deputy head of US Africa Command (AFRICOM) cautioned that similar partnerships with military-led governments in West Africa have failed to improve security. Lieutenant General John Brennan said they were concerned that Russia wants to expand the model it has used in the Sahel to elsewhere across the continent.
articles.body:
Madagascar

The United States has warned Madagascar against strengthening its military ties with Russia.

The deputy head of US Africa Command (AFRICOM) cautioned that similar partnerships with military-led governments in West Africa have failed to improve security.

Lieutenant General John Brennan said they were concerned that Russia wants to expand the model it has used in the Sahel to elsewhere across the continent.

"Madagascar sits in a location that is extremely important, as is Mozambique, and we don't want to see those models be applied in those two locations," he said.

Brennan highlighted the strategic value of the Mozambique Channel, the shipping route between those two countries, calling it vital to international trade.

The waterway has become more important as the Middle East war forces shipping through different routes.

Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso, all under military rule, have turned to Russia for support in their fight against jihadist groups, distancing themselves from Western partners.

Brennan's comments came as Madagascar's military government also deepens ties with Moscow.

Russia has expanded its cooperation with the island nation since the army seized power last year, supplying it with weapons and instructors from its paramilitary force, Africa Corps.

In one of Colonel Michael Randrianirina’s first official visits after seizing power, he travelled to Moscow on a plane chartered by Russia to meet President Vladimir Putin.

Brennan said that while US partners were "free to partner with whom they wish", they should understand "the risks associated with that”.

He described Moscow’s approach as "largely ineffective" in the Sahel and east Africa, warning it could further destabilise the region if replicated elsewhere.

Brennan said he believed Russia’s "real motives" were to "control their natural resources, predate on their population, and then infringe on their sovereignty".

articles.title: Three Iran-backed suspects plotted attacks including RAF Fairford incident, US says
articles.summary: The US Department of Justice says the men were involved in a string of plots, including a major incident near the UK airbase that is used by US armed forces.
articles.preview: The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has announced charges against three Iran-backed operatives that it alleges were involved in a string of plots in the US and Europe. The DOJ said Iranian agents most recently "orchestrated a terrorist plot at an air force base in the United Kingdom", saying they were involved in the major incident in September near RAF Fairford in the UK, where US armed forces were stationed. The three men have been accused by the DOJ of being involved in 18 attacks and attempted attacks, including in London, Amsterdam and Paris.
articles.body:
The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has announced charges against three Iran-backed operatives that it alleges were involved in a string of plots in the US and Europe.

The DOJ said Iranian agents most recently "orchestrated a terrorist plot at an air force base in the United Kingdom", saying they were involved in the major incident in September near RAF Fairford in the UK, where US armed forces were stationed.

The three men have been accused by the DOJ of being involved in 18 attacks and attempted attacks, including in London, Amsterdam and Paris. Some of the incidents were said to be directed by the men over FaceTime.

The DOJ said they acted in the name of the group Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI).

Iranian Mohsen Mohajeri, Iraqi national Mohammad Ali al-Hassani and dual Iranian-Iraqi citizen Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi were charged in an indictment unsealed on Tuesday, the DOJ said.

The DOJ said that most recently, al-Hassani "orchestrated a terrorist plot" at RAF Fairford - where on 27 September a major incident was declared after suspicious vans were reported near the base.

Seven men have been arrested in the UK over the incident at RAF Fairford.

Iran has strongly denied any involvement.

Al-Hassani and Mohajeri were allegedly both in Iran at the time of the incident, the indictment claims.

Meanwhile, al-Saadi was coordinating with the pair through third parties from a prison in New York, where he is awaiting trial on previous charges after being arrested in August, it adds.

US court records show that al-Saadi is due in court on 19 November, though it is not clear whether this status conference - which is usually a routine scheduled appearance - relates to the new charges or the previous ones. The BBC has asked the Southern District of New York for comment.

Mohajeri and al-Hassani are not in custody, two sources told the BBC's US partner CBS News.

The BBC has asked the DOJ for comment on the suspected whereabouts of the two men not in US custody.

In the DOJ's statement detailing the indictments, it said: "Of the 18 terrorist attacks in the spring of 2026 for which HAYI claimed responsibility in Europe, seven took place in the UK."

It added that the attacks involved "arsons, explosives, and in one instance, a near-fatal stabbing in London of two Jewish men, including a dual US-British citizen".

Two Jewish men were stabbed in Golders Green, north London, in April. A suspect is due to stand trial next year.

The indictment also details an arson attack on a Jewish charity in London on 17 April, which allegedly saw al-Hassani "directing" an individual over FaceTime.

On 17 April , a building previously used by Jewish Futures, an educational charity, was set alight in Hendon, north-west London.

The following day, the DOJ said al-Hassani participated in another video call with an individual carrying out an attack on a synagogue in London.

On 18 April, Kenton United Synagogue in Harrow was targeted in an arson attack. A 17-year-old boy pleaded guilty to the incident earlier this year.

The indictment also claims the three were involved in attacks on the Bank of New York Mellon building in Amsterdam on 15 March and on the Bank of America building in Paris on 28 March.

It added that the trio tried to carry out attacks on "Jewish institutions in the US", including attempting to target a synagogue in Manhattan, New York in March or April.

"This eight-count indictment shows the determination of Iran to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the US," FBI Director Kash Patel said.

He added that one of the three "allegedly sent coded messages to assist in future acts of violence" from detention.

Patel said the accused were involved in nearly 20 attempted attacks in support of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Iran-backed Iraqi militia Kataib Hezbollah.

RAF Fairford

A major incident was declared on 27 September near the UK's RAF Fairford base, in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire, after three suspicious vans were seen near the airbase.

No explosive materials were found in the vans, but a quantity of petrol was seized.

The DOJ said that in August, al-Hassani "allegedly directed and paid associates" in the UK to "conduct preparatory steps and arrange logistics for the RAF Fairford terrorist plot".

On 22 August, al-Hassani paid one individual to "perform pre-operational surveillance of RAF Fairford's perimeter", the department said.

In September, al-Hassani paid several people to help him prepare for the plot, the DOJ also alleged.

According to its statement, this included "procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel".

The suspects then gave the vans an appearance of being used by a fuel delivery business and a swimming pool supply business, the DOJ stated.

"On 26 September, al-Hassani allegedly tasked individuals to drive three vans, some of which were later determined to contain barrels of fuel, to the RAF Fairford base."

The DOJ also said al-Hassani was "in frequent communication" with the van drivers and helped to direct them where to drive.

"At least two of the three vans, while en route to the perimeter of RAF Fairford, encountered a security roadblock and were not allowed to proceed on their intended route," it added.

It was in the very early hours of 27 September, that the vans were spotted by a local farmer who was heading home from a party, and called the police.

The Iranian embassy in London has said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" what it called "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the incident.

Two British nationals appeared in court last month in connection with the alleged Iran-linked plot.

The US withdrew all its bombers from RAF Fairford after the incident, with President Donald Trump citing "some threats" to the base as the reason.

RAF Fairford has been used by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.

In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from there to the Middle East for "defensive" strikes on Iran.

In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".

articles.body:
Abdel-Malek, the captain and goalkeeper of Gaza Sports Club, recently played in the Thousand Martyrs Cup final.

Gaza holds final of tournament honouring more than 1,000 slain athletes

Palestinian footballer Mahmoud Kamal Fares Abdel-Malek has been killed in an Israeli air strike on Gaza, the Palestinian Football Association (PFA) has confirmed.

The PFA said Abdel-Malek, the captain and goalkeeper of Gaza Sports Club, was targeted in Tuesday’s attack on Gaza City’s southern Sabra neighbourhood.

The 20-year-old was the 1,017th person involved in sport to be killed in Gaza in Israel’s genocidal war on the enclave, according to figures provided by the PFA.

Abdel-Malek’s death came five days after he played in the final of the Gaza and Northern Gaza division of the Thousand Martyrs Cup, a tournament named after the more than 1,000 athletes and sports officials killed in the Strip since October 2023.

“Club legend and goalkeeper of the first team Mahmoud Kamal Fares Abdel-Malik was martyred moments ago,” the club wrote in a social media post announcing his death.

Gaza Sports Club finished as runners-up in the final of the tournament that Al Jazeera covered last week.

More than 200 clubs competed, including 146 from the occupied West Bank, 44 from Gaza, and 36 from Palestinian refugee camps in Lebanon.

The tournament kicked off simultaneously in the three locations.

PFA President Jibril Rajoub said the event showed that Palestinians had not lost their “national will”.

“Nor have we lost our belief that sport will remain a symbol of hope and life,” he added.

Abdel-Malek’s death comes days after Israeli forces killed 15-year-old Mohammad Nidal Barbak on Friday, shooting him while he was playing football with his friends in the al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis.

The incident has highlighted FIFA’s inaction towards Israel, despite its multiple breaches of the global football body’s anti-discrimination rules.

In March, the PFA called for the Israeli Football Association (IFA) to receive a ban after a report by FIFA’s disciplinary committee found that the IFA “failed to take meaningful action against Beitar Jerusalem” for “persistent and well-documented racist behaviour”.

“We maintain our right and continue our efforts to ensure that the Israeli Football Association is expelled from all international institutions,” Rajoub, who also heads the Palestine Olympic Committee, said at the time.

On the alleged criminal activity of Israeli sports officials, Rajoub said he was referring to instances of players killed during the three years of genocide in Gaza, and the destruction of many of the territory’s sports facilities.

Israeli attacks have devastated Gaza’s sports infrastructure, destroying stadiums, clubs, sports halls and academies as well as bulldozing several sports facilities, Palestinian sports officials say.

The human losses and destruction have left Palestinian sport in an “existential” crisis, according to Palestinian Sports Media Federation Secretary-General Mustafa Siam.

Israel has destroyed more than 50 of Gaza’s 56 sports clubs and about 20 five-a-side football fields established by the PFA with support from FIFA, he told the Anadolu news agency in August.

At least 74,645 Palestinians have been killed since October 7, 2023, while 175,978 have been injured, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health.

articles.title: Indonesia's vice president resigns amid signs ruling alliance is fraying
articles.summary: The news comes at a turbulent time for Prabowo, who faces a growing rift with his predecessor Joko Widodo.
articles.preview: Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has submitted his resignation, an aide has told the BBC, in a move which could further strain the political alliance that helped propel President Prabowo Subianto to power. It comes after Indonesia's Supreme Court ruled that a high-school document used during Gibran's 2024 election campaign was invalid. The ruling prompted more than 100 lawmakers to support a parliamentary initiative that could have paved the way for proceedings to impeach Gibran.
articles.body:
Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has submitted his resignation, an aide has told the BBC, in a move which could further strain the political alliance that helped propel President Prabowo Subianto to power.

It comes after Indonesia's Supreme Court ruled that a high-school document used during Gibran's 2024 election campaign was invalid.

The ruling prompted more than 100 lawmakers to support a parliamentary initiative that could have paved the way for proceedings to impeach Gibran.

The aide, Budi Arie, said Gibran's resignation letter was submitted directly to Prabowo on Wednesday. It remains unclear if it has been accepted.

Gibran has long faced controversy over whether his high school qualifications met legal requirements to run for office.

Having studied in Singapore and Australia, he had used an Indonesian equivalence certificate to demonstrate his educational credentials.

Indonesian law requires vice-presidents to have completed senior secondary school or its equivalent, but the Supreme Court found no evidence to prove Gibran had graduated.

"No evidence was found to show Gibran had a foreign diploma or certificate that could serve as the basis for equivalency with a senior high school or equivalent qualification," it said.

It also considered a Constitutional Court ruling from earlier in October which came to the same conclusion.

Gibran previously argued that undertaking university education was sufficient proof that he had completed senior high school.

On Tuesday, he asked for the chance to challenge the ruling and be given the opportunity to prove the legitimacy of his education credentials, State Secretary Prasetyo Hadi said.

Gibran's ascension to Prabowo's ticket in the 2024 election was part of an alliance formed between his father, outgoing president Joko Widodo - known as Jokowi - and Prabowo, his erstwhile bitter rival.

Gibran was 36 at the time, and only became eligible for candidacy after a controversial ruling by the Constitutional Court, which exempted him from the minimum age requirement of 40.

His resignation comes as tensions between Jokowi and Prabowo appear to have flared.

Since taking the presidency, Prabowo has shown little interest in pushing ahead with Jokowi's legacy project: the construction of Nusantara, a new capital. Instead, he has focused much of the state's resources on his own flagship programme to provide free school meals across the country.

In a series of personnel reshuffles over the past year, Prabowo has also shifted many Jokowi loyalists into new roles, including long-serving finance minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati.

Last week, authorities arrested presidential chief of staff Listyo Sigit Prabowo - no relation - on suspicions of wiretapping the president.

Prabowo sacked Listyo a day later, in what many pointed to as a sign of a crumbling alliance: Listyo, who formerly served as the national police chief, is widely considered a long-time ally of Jokowi.

Within the government, allegiances seem to be shifting. On Monday, three members of Prabowo's cabinet collectively resigned from the party led by Kaesang Pangarep, Jokowi's youngest son, citing their desire to focus on their duties in Prabowo's administration.

All this is unfolding at a particularly turbulent period in Prabowo's presidency. The free school meals programme is struggling for funding, parts of Indonesia have recently battled the country's worst wildfires in a decade, and the national stock market faces crisis amid allegations of widespread market manipulation.

On Tuesday, students across the country staged demonstrations to protest against the government's handling of a range of issues, including the environmental crisis and corruption.

articles.summary: The fine came after President Lula's coalition filed a complaint. The court said there was no evidence of intent to influence the election. Meta said it will defend itself against "false allegations."

The court said there was no evidence of intent to influence the election. Meta said it will defend itself against "false allegations." Brazil's top electoral court has ordered Meta to pay 7.5 million reais ($1.34 million; €1.22 million) for failing to fully comply with judicial orders during last month's presidential election.
articles.body:
Brazil's electoral court fines Meta $1.3M for noncompliance

November 11, 2026

The fine came after President Lula's coalition filed a complaint. The court said there was no evidence of intent to influence the election. Meta said it will defend itself against "false allegations."

Brazil's top electoral court has ordered Meta to pay 7.5 million reais ($1.34 million; €1.22 million) for failing to fully comply with judicial orders during last month's presidential election.

However, the judicial body has so far found no evidence that Meta deliberately acted to influence the election outcome.

Ahead of the runoff vote on October 25, leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's coalition filed a complaint, accusing Meta of "algorithmic manipulation" favoring his far-right rival Flavio Bolsonaro.

Platforms owned by Meta include Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.

Meta told the court last month that it had implemented measures to guarantee equal treatment for both campaigns.

Meta lacked transparency, court says

The Superior Electoral Court (TSE) unanimously ruled on Tuesday to impose the 7.5 million reais fine on the US tech giant.

Meta missed deadlines and lacked transparency in its investigation, the court said.

On the other hand, the court's reporting judge Marco Aurelio Belizze wrote in his ruling that there were no preliminary evidence indicating that any intentional actions were taken to influence the election.

"That conclusion would require robust evidence, to be produced through the appropriate legal proceedings," he said.

According to Bellizze, the fine was based on Meta's overall handling of the court orders, including delays, incomplete disclosures, and challenges in verifying some of the information it provided.

In a statement on Wednesday, Meta strongly denied the court's ruling.

"We will continue to present the facts and defend ourselves against false allegations in the ongoing legal proceedings," Meta said in a statement on Wednesday.

Lula vows to rein in social media

Lula defeated Bolsonaro in a tight run-off in October 25 with him winning 51.7% of the vote against Bolsonaro's 48.2%.

In his victory speech, Lula urged more regulation of big tech platforms after allegations that Meta interfered in the race.

"We had to overcome foreign interference in the election, coming from outside through digital platforms that we will have to regulate," he said.

articles.summary: The United States has raised concerns over Madagascar's growing military cooperation with Russia, warning that similar partnerships in West Africa have failed to curb militant violence.

Lieutenant General John Brennan, deputy commander of US Africa Command, said Washington was concerned that Russia could extend its influence beyond the Sahel, where military-led governments have increasingly turned to Moscow for security assistance.
articles.body:
Madagascar

The United States has raised concerns over Madagascar's growing military cooperation with Russia, warning that similar partnerships in West Africa have failed to curb militant violence.

Lieutenant General John Brennan, deputy commander of US Africa Command, said Washington was concerned that Russia could extend its influence beyond the Sahel, where military-led governments have increasingly turned to Moscow for security assistance.

Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger have cut military ties with traditional Western allies and sought Russian support in their fight against jihadist groups. However, attacks have continued despite the shift.

Brennan warned against extending what he described as the "Sahel model" to Madagascar and neighbouring Mozambique, citing their strategic importance to international shipping.

The Mozambique Channel, which separates Madagascar from mainland Africa, is a major maritime trade route. Washington is concerned that militants operating in northern Mozambique could increasingly threaten shipping as they develop maritime capabilities.

Russia has supplied Madagascar with weapons and military instructors since the country's military takeover in 2025.

President Michaël Randrianirina has continued to pursue closer relations with Moscow. The two countries recently signed agreements covering defence, trade and tourism during a Russia-Africa summit.

Randrianirina also travelled to Moscow in February, marking the first official visit by a Malagasy leader in nearly five decades.

Madagascar has not publicly responded to the US warning.

articles.summary: A deadly sandbank collapse buried families alive in Deir el-Balah, as survivors describe desperate rescue attempts.

articles.body:
A deadly sandbank collapse buried displaced families alive in Deir el-Balah, as survivors describe desperate rescue attempts.

Deir el-Balah, Gaza Strip – Gaza is dealing with the cleanup of catastrophic flooding after storms submerged displacement camps and war-destroyed cities.

Heavy rain has directly affected 106,000 people in Gaza, according to UNICEF, with thousands of tents for displaced Palestinians submerged under water and latrines overflowing into camps.

The floods also brought death: a sandbank under pressure from heavy rain collapsed at the Ard al-Ribat displacement camp in Deir el-Balah, central Gaza, on Sunday evening, killing three children and a woman.

Without excavation equipment, residents had to dig through the sand with their bare hands to reach people trapped under debris. When darkness came, they used flashlights on their mobile phones to search for survivors.

Zahira al-Sahar, 58, was preparing to sleep in her tent in the camp on Sunday when she and her 28-year-old daughter were almost entombed in the collapse.

“I was lying in my bedding when something suddenly pushed me and came down on top of me,” al-Sahar told Al Jazeera. “The sand reached up to my neck. My daughter was beside me, and she was almost completely buried.”

Her sons came to the rescue. “I told them: ‘Pull your sister out first, then come back for me.’ They pulled her out, then came back and rescued me,” she said.

Meanwhile, in a neighbouring tent, members of the al-Nabhan family were also buried in the sandbank’s collapse.

“[When I realised] I started screaming and calling for people to come and help,” al-Sahar said. “I told everyone that our neighbours had been buried. We kept shouting: ‘Please, save them. Our neighbours are gone.’”

But the family did not respond to the rescuers’ calls. Eight-year-old Salah, his six-year-old sister Maryam, and their mother, Tahrir, 36, who was five months pregnant, were among the dead. Their father, Ahmed, who was only recently released from Israeli detention, is the family’s sole survivor.

“[Ahmed al-Nabhan] and his wife had been very happy after he came out of prison. They were looking forward to having another child in a few months,” said Suhaib Abu Darabi, 32, who was among neighbours who rushed to the site to help save them.

Abu Darabi said the collapse sounded like an explosion and was followed by screaming. The site was exposed to the elements and on unstable ground and collapsed after just a few minutes of rain. By the time neighbours reached the area, they found two tents completely buried under debris.

Abu Darabi said residents were digging with whatever tools they could find.

“We managed to clear some of the rubble, but we could not save the people trapped underneath. The scale of the collapse was far beyond what the residents here could handle, given the lack of resources,” Abu Darabi told Al Jazeera.

“The tents that collapsed beneath the embankment are what the world saw. But what people did not see was that all these tents fell to the ground that night. Residents had to repair whatever they could so they could continue living in them.”

In the neighbouring al-Zein family’s tent, four-year-old Habiba was killed, while her mother, Reem, and brother Ibrahim remain in intensive care.

The scale of the damage caused by this winter’s first storm, which began on November 6, was significant and has exposed the dangers faced by families living in tents with little protection from extreme weather.

This is the fourth winter since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began, in October 2023, and hundreds of thousands of people are living in tattered tents or makeshift shelters that have been exposed to the elements for years.

More than 26,000 households had reported damage to their shelters or other belongings by November 8, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported. The UN estimated that about 1.4 million people, or 65 percent of Gaza’s population, were living in tents or makeshift shelters when the storms hit.

The danger is only compounded by the extensive destruction of Gaza’s infrastructure from Israeli strikes. Drainage networks have been severely damaged, roads and access routes remain in poor condition, and municipalities lack sufficient equipment to remove accumulated rainwater and respond to emergencies.

Gaza’s Government Media Office described the Deir el-Balah sandbank collapse as a humanitarian disaster.

It said it held Israel, the United States administration and the international community responsible and the blocking of proper shelters, construction materials, mobile homes, fuel and spare parts was a factor in the deadly floods.

The media office also said the failure of the so-called Board of Peace and the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza to act in the crisis also raised “serious questions about the purpose of these bodies”, which have been accused of working with Israel to continue its siege on Gaza.

The Board of Peace said in a statement this week that it had urged Israel to allow essential supplies such as temporary shelters and drainage equipment to enter the enclave.

Aid organisations have also repeatedly called for the entry of shelter materials and equipment needed to repair damaged tents and infrastructure to avoid a repeat of this past week’s deadly events.

Shaima al-Daour, 22, a displaced woman from northern Gaza who works as a nurse in the Ard al-Ribat camp, was also among those who rushed to help the injured.

“I tried to resuscitate a young child who was pulled out from under the rubble, but he had internal bleeding. I tried, but there was no response,” she said.

Al-Daour said another boy, aged 15, was brought to her with difficulty breathing. She opened his airway and he began to breathe, but his pulse was weak. With no ambulance readily available, she called on people around her to find any means of transport to get him to the hospital.

“I was surrounded by men, shouting at them: ‘Does anyone have a tuk-tuk? A cart? Anything to carry him?’ What I saw was unbearable. I could not save the little child in front of me,” she said.

“We need shelter and land where people can live safely. We also need equipment so that, God forbid, if something happens again, there is something available to help us.”

Al-Daour said she is still in shock by what she witnessed and is terrified by the prospect of the impending winter.

“I still cannot get over what happened,” she said. “Have the people of Gaza not experienced every possible way of dying? Have some compassion for us. Just have some compassion for us, people of the world,” she said.

articles.body:
Anthony Albanese said governments had a “solemn responsibility” to act on climate change in a historic speech to the UN’s climate summit, but one which failed to mention the fossil fuels driving the crisis.

The Australia prime minister landed in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya on Wednesday morning where the Cop31 talks are being presided over by his climate change minister, Chris Bowen, but hosted by Turkey.

Only moments before Albanese spoke, on the same stage the UN secretary general Antonio Guterres said unambiguously that keeping the 1.5C temperature goal alive “means no new coal”.

In a packed conference room, Turkey put on an opening ceremony of whirling traditional dancers, booming music and a film shot around the world with characters saying “We need to talk”.

“This is an historic moment for my country,” said Albanese, adding Australia was “proud to be a leader on climate action.”

“Proud to be a renewable energy leader, creating the clean industries, businesses and jobs of the future. And proud to be here fighting for the interests of our Pacific family,” he said.

Australia had pushed for a role at the climate summit, he said, “because we wanted to speak for the people of the world who need urgent action, including those from our Pacific family”.

Australia is the world’s second largest exporter of coal for burning in power stations and the largest exporter of coal for steelmaking. A fifth of the world’s exported LNG comes from Australia.

Albanese pointed to “significant successes” for the country on climate change, including doubling renewable energy generation in six years that accounted for half of the country’s electricity, and building one of the world’s biggest rooftop solar and battery markets.

Guterres and several countries are pushing for the talks to progress a proposal from last year’s Cop hosts, Brazil, for countries to develop detailed plans to move away from fossil fuels.

Guterres told the conference: “Leaders – and in particular those from developed countries – cannot keep expanding fossil fuel production while claiming to be committed to 1.5 degrees.”

He said to keep the globally-agreed goal of limiting global heating to 1.5C within reach, coal power had to fall by at least 75% by 2035.

Unabated coal power – that is, coal generated without safely capturing the carbon dioxide emissions – “must be all but phased out” by 2040, and oil and gas use cut by a third, he said.

“Every government must align its policies, investments and infrastructure plans accordingly. That starts with credible national roadmaps to transition away from fossil fuels — protecting workers and communities.

“That means no new coal. No new oil and gas infrastructure that puts 1.5 degrees further out of reach.”

Guterres has consistently called out fossil fuel production and lobbying and the lack of action on climate change as temperatures and weather extremes have worsened.

Adam Bandt, the former Greens leader and now chief executive of the Australian Conservation Foundation, said Albanese had “bluntly ignored” the secretary general’s message.

“The prime minister’s speech wasn’t just a missed opportunity, but by refusing to rein in coal and gas expansion or even mention it once, it was a snub to the secretary general’s call to tell the truth,” he said.

“At this summit, Australia is getting repeatedly called out for opening new coal and gas mines and the government can’t dodge it forever.”

Bill Hare, the Australian chief executive of Climate Analytics and a veteran of Cop meetings, said it was “disturbing” that Albanese had failed to mention fossil fuels.

As a major fossil fuel exporter, he said a “responsible leader” would have talked about developing a pathway out of fossil fuels.

“It still seems to be a dirty word. It’s the elephant in the room,” he said, pointing to 38 fossil projects approved by the Albanese government since it was elected in 2022.

Australia and Turkey are seeking support for a global goal to see 35% of final-use energy coming from electricity by 2035 – up from about a fifth today.

Speaking during a roll-call of heads of state and world leaders, Bowen said the world was asking if multilateralism could rise to a “polycrisis” of climate change, energy security, conflict and the power demands of artificial intelligence.

“Is international cooperation still a way forward? This fortnight we can answer those legitimate concerns and questions with a simple answer: Yes,” said Bowen.

Democratic Republic Of Congo

DR Congo President Felix Tshisekedi has enacted a law that paves the way for a change to the constitution, condemned by the opposition as an attempt by the president to cling onto power.

The law eases the rules around holding a referendum on constitutional matters. It was enacted in an order read on national television overnight Tuesday to Wednesday. Tshisekedi, 63, has been in power since 2019 and under the current constitution has to step down at the end of his second five-year term at the end of 2028.

Opposition parties have joined forces in recent months to stand against his attempt to change the constitution and open the way for him to run for a third term. Tshisekedi declared at a rare news conference in early May that he had "not sought a third term" but said: "If people want me to have a third term, I will accept."

Demonstrations called by the opposition to protest a "constitutional coup" took place in June and September in the capital, Kinshasa, and other cities. Weakened and fragmented after Tshisekedi's landslide victory in the 2023 election, the opposition -- which has recently grouped together in a platform called C64 -- has struggled however to rally large numbers of people in the streets.

It comes with much of the eastern part of the vast central African country riven by conflict, where the Rwanda-backed M23 armed group seized swathes of territory last year.

JAKARTA: Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has resigned, an aide said on Wednesday (Nov 11), a move that risks further political turbulence in Southeast Asia's largest economy.
articles.body:
He has come under intense scrutiny following Constitutional Court and Supreme Court rulings last month that his education documents did not meet election requirements.

JAKARTA: Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has resigned, an aide said on Wednesday (Nov 11), a move that risks further political turbulence in Southeast Asia's largest economy.

Gibran, the 39-year-old son of former President Joko Widodo, has come under intense scrutiny following Constitutional Court and Supreme Court rulings last month that his education documents did not meet election requirements.

The aide, Budi Arie Setiadi, told Reuters that Gibran had tendered his resignation to President Prabowo Subianto earlier on Wednesday.

Separately, two sources at the parliamentary upper house, which will oversee the process of approving his resignation and selecting a replacement, told Reuters that he will submit his resignation letter to the upper house on Thursday morning.

Gibran's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The controversy has unfolded amid a widening rift between Widodo, also known as Jokowi, and Prabowo.

Jokowi’s support was instrumental in securing the Prabowo-Gibran ticket's victory in the 2024 election.

Gibran met Prabowo for two-and-a-half hours on Tuesday morning, during which he expressed an intention to resign amid mounting pressure over his educational qualifications, according to presidential spokesperson Prasetyo Hadi.

While Gibran has not publicly confirmed that he intends to resign, he told reporters later on Tuesday afternoon that Prabowo had advised him to continue fighting his case over his educational records, including seeking a judicial review of a Supreme Court ruling.

On Oct 30, Indonesia's Supreme Court annulled Gibran's overseas high school education equivalency certificate less than a month after the Constitutional Court found insufficient documentary evidence establishing that Gibran’s foreign schooling met the relevant qualification requirements.

Parliament also convened on Tuesday after a month-long recess, with 50 lawmakers from six parliamentary factions backing a proposal to exercise the House of Representatives' right to express an opinion, a mechanism that could potentially lead to impeachment proceedings against Gibran.

Earlier on Wednesday, 120 parliamentarians from eight factions signed the proposal, paving the way for Gibran's impeachment.

articles.preview: Nissan lowered its annual car sales outlook due to weak demand and mounting competition in China, where buyers are shifting to locally made electric vehicles faster than it expected. The Japanese manufacturer now projects at most 3 million vehicle deliveries this year, from 3.15 million previously, it said Wednesday. Nissan reported second-quarter operating profit that came in significantly below analyst expectations. “China remains our biggest challenge,” Chief Executive Officer Ivan Espinosa told reporters in Yokohama.
articles.body:
Nissan lowered its annual car sales outlook due to weak demand and mounting competition in China, where buyers are shifting to locally made electric vehicles faster than it expected.

The Japanese manufacturer now projects at most 3 million vehicle deliveries this year, from 3.15 million previously, it said Wednesday. Nissan reported second-quarter operating profit that came in significantly below analyst expectations.

“China remains our biggest challenge,” Chief Executive Officer Ivan Espinosa told reporters in Yokohama.

The results show how far the embattled Japanese carmaker still has to go in its efforts to come back from its worst financial crisis. Nissan has started a broad cost-cutting campaign that includes cutting jobs and shutting down factories. But it still faces sizeable debt obligations and is struggling to compete with the industry’s shift toward EVs with complex software, particularly in China.

Nissan’s sales in the world’s biggest car market fell 15% during the first half of the fiscal year. The company is looking to turn things around by adding more EVs and plug-in hybrid cars to its lineup, some of which will be exported to other markets.

Business was better elsewhere. Deliveries increased 6.3% in Japan and 2.1% in North America — regions where the shift to EVs is happening at a slower pace.

Nissan’s operating profit came in at ¥2.12 billion ($13.3 million) for the three months through September. That’s well below the ¥49.3 billion projected by analysts. The company maintained its full-year financial forecast on expectations that profitability will improve in the second half due to new models and higher sales volumes.

Nissan will announce a new business strategy in February that will go beyond its current restructuring plan, Espinosa said.

articles.title: Iran classes Argentina navy, air force as 'terrorist organizations'
articles.summary: In a tit-for-tat move, Iran has said it now considers Argentina's navy and air force as "terrorist organizations." Tehran claimed Buenos Aires is responsible for further consequences.
articles.preview: November 11, 2026 In a tit-for-tat move, Iran has said it now considers Argentina's navy and air force as "terrorist organizations." Tehran claimed Buenos Aires is responsible for further consequences. Iran's Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday that it classified Argentina's navy and air force as "terrorist organizations." In early April, Argentina designated Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as a "terrorist organization," as US President Donald Trump pressured his allies to do so following the war on Iran.
articles.body:
November 11, 2026

In a tit-for-tat move, Iran has said it now considers Argentina's navy and air force as "terrorist organizations." Tehran claimed Buenos Aires is responsible for further consequences.

Iran's Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday that it classified Argentina's navy and air force as "terrorist organizations."

In early April, Argentina designated Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as a "terrorist organization," as US President Donald Trump pressured his allies to do so following the war on Iran.

Tehran's designation came "based on the principle of reciprocity," Iran's Foreign Ministry said in a statement.

"It is evident that the responsibility for all consequences arising from this matter will lie with the Argentine government," the ministry added, without a mention of Argentina's army.

Iran passed a legislation in 2019 that grants retaliatory measures against states that designate its military as a terrorist group.

Argentina holds Hezbollah responsible for deadly attacks

Argentina said in April that it had taken action against the IRGC because of its support for the Lebanon-based militant group Hezbollah.

Buenos Aires holds Hezbollah responsible for the 1994 bombing of the AMIA Jewish community center, which killed 85 people.

IRGC classified as a terrorist group by many countries

IRGC was established at the end of Iran's 1979 Islamic Revolution as an elite armed militia whose role was to protect the then embryonic Shiite clerical regime.

Over the years, it has morphed into a vast economic and political empire. Rather than the elected president, the force answers directly to Iran's supreme leader.

The United States, the European Union, and the United Kingdom, along with other countries, classify the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps as a terrorist organization.

articles.body:
Antalya, Turkey – An international nongovernment environmental group on Tuesday gave Japan and eight other countries its Fossil of the Day award for inadequate climate action, citing their leaders’ failure to attend the ongoing U.N. climate talks in Turkey.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is absent from the two-day leaders’ meeting of the climate talks through Thursday for scheduling reasons, marking the third straight year that a Japanese prime minister has skipped the summit.

From the Group of Seven countries, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham is the only leader expected to attend the summit.

The Climate Action Network said that the absence of the leaders from the meeting could delay the progress of negotiations and raise concerns that climate change measures would be put on the back burner.

The fossil award will be presented daily until the conference ends on Nov. 20.

articles.title: Nelle scuole un attacco ibrido 'con l'obiettivo di minare la democrazia'
articles.summary: Criminologo Sapienza ed esperto Ue: 'minaccia immateriale che mina la fiducia sociale'
articles.preview: 'Un attacco ibrido con l'obiettivo di minare la democrazia: "un attacco di questo tipo è diverso dalla guerra ibrida e non è nemmeno terrorismo: è una minaccia immateriale che ha conseguenze a livello sociale, cognitivo e istituzionale. Sfrutta cioè il funzionamento ordinario della società per moltiplicare un effetto destabilizzante", dice all'ANSA Arije Antinori, professore di Criminologia alla Sapienza Università di Roma ed esperto dell'Eu Knowledge Hub on Prevention of Radicalisation (Eukh), l'iniziativa della Commissione Europea lanciata nel 2024…
articles.body:
'Un attacco ibrido con l'obiettivo di minare la democrazia: "un attacco di questo tipo è diverso dalla guerra ibrida e non è nemmeno terrorismo: è una minaccia immateriale che ha conseguenze a livello sociale, cognitivo e istituzionale. Sfrutta cioè il funzionamento ordinario della società per moltiplicare un effetto destabilizzante", dice all'ANSA Arije Antinori, professore di Criminologia alla Sapienza Università di Roma ed esperto dell'Eu Knowledge Hub on Prevention of Radicalisation (Eukh), l'iniziativa della Commissione Europea lanciata nel 2024 per contrastare estremismo violento e terrorismo negli Stati membri.

La scelta delle scuole come obiettivo, osserva , "è determinante perché la scuola è la porta d'ingresso di un sistema interdipendente costituito da famiglie, istituzioni, media e opinione pubblica, che si sorreggono attraverso un rapporto di fiducia". Attacchi a costo limitato come questi colpiscono, "il sistema di relazioni" e "sovraccaricano le istituzioni di compiti". In pratica, si attacca la sicurezza della vita quotidiama. Questa, osserva Antinori, "dipende da presupposti che raramente vengono messi in discussione. Per esempio, per tutti la scuola è un luogo protetto, le emergenze sono percepite come eventi sporadici, ci si fida delle comunicazioni ufficiali". Gli attacchi ibridi "non solo diffondono paura e incertezza, ma fanno in modo che l'insicurezza venga percepita come un fatto ordinario: così si colpisce il sistema di relazioni interno alla società". Le conseguenze, rileva , hanno una "portata sistemica": attaccando il sistema di relazioni ,ottengono un effetto destabilizzante e generano "una perturbazione sociale che mina le relazioni di fiducia".

Il problema più grande degli attacchi ibridi, prosegue Antinori, "è che una volta evidenziate le vulnerabilità, altri attori possono sfruttare la situazione con attacchi opportunistici ibridi" verso obiettivi legati alla quotidianità, come è avvenuto recentemente in voli di linea, supermercati e scuole. Se qualcuno innesca l'attacco, altri possono intervenire successivamente, compresi gruppi della criminalità organizzata, fino a "indebolire e sfilacciare il tessuto sociale delle democrazie all'interno", osserva.

Se le infrastrutture critiche tradizionali erano energia luce, gas, acqua o connessioni internet, per gli attacchi ibridi "tutto ciò che è legato alla quotidianità può diventare un'infrastruttura critica, con i conseguenti costi operativi di gestione e sicurezza". Si tende a "mandare in crisi il nostro sistema fino a indurci a fare passi indietro nei processi democratici". E' una situazione che nessuno Stato, nemmeno i più avanzati, è in grado di governare. Reagire è possibile "lavorando moltissimo sul piano della resilienza, ripristinando un contesto di fiducia nella comunità in modo forte e considerando la disinformazione una minaccia sul piano politico". Bisogna prepararsi, conclude l'esperto, perché in futuro attacchi come quelli recenti potrebbero colpire anche in un'unica giornata.

articles.title: Russia-Ukraine talks turn to post-war security but end without breakthrough
articles.summary: Talks in Abu Dhabi centred around Europe's security framework, with US envoys due to meet Putin and Zelensky on Thursday.
articles.preview: Trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine have concluded after a second day. Although the American side said they saw "some openings", there was no hint of any breakthroughs to end the nearly five year-long war sparked by Russia's invasion. However, both Moscow and Kyiv confirmed that a large-scale prisoner of war exchange was in the works and could be carried out soon.
articles.body:
Trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine have concluded after a second day.

Although the American side said they saw "some openings", there was no hint of any breakthroughs to end the nearly five year-long war sparked by Russia's invasion.

However, both Moscow and Kyiv confirmed that a large-scale prisoner of war exchange was in the works and could be carried out soon.

Davyd Arakhamia from Ukraine's negotiating team said that this round of talks - the first since February - "was one of the hardest."

"I believe the Russians came with very strict directives, so it was extremely difficult to soften the discussion," he said. But he added that he felt "good momentum" and urged for a second round of talks to be organised as soon as possible.

Comments by Kremlin negotiator Vladimir Medinsky were less conciliatory. "Right now... a lot depends on Ukraine, on the position of the US, and on whether Europe comes to its senses," he said.

After the talks it was announced that on Thursday US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner - President Donald Trump's son-in-law - would travel to Moscow to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin, and then to Dublin to speak to Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky.

The meetings in Abu Dhabi had been framed as centred around the "security architecture" of Europe.

For Kyiv, this may include reassurances that allies will come to its aid if Ukraine comes under attack again, despite the country not being a Nato member.

For Moscow, a reworked "security framework" is likely to include a limit to the influence of Nato in eastern Europe - a central concern for the Kremlin since the alliance's eastward expansion.

Earlier this week Kushner said the US hoped to "create a new framework" of security between Ukraine, Russia and Europe that could "secure lasting peace", while the Kremlin's Medinsky said the world needed a "new" and "fair" security system.

That framework would serve as "a new Yalta and Potsdam", Medinsky said, referring to the 1940s summits in which the victorious Allied powers carved up post-war Europe into spheres of influence.

Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US administration's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin.

Representatives of Britain, Nato and various EU countries were also in Abu Dhabi and met with US and Ukrainian negotiators, but the Kremlin - with whom the EU does not officially communicate - said its delegation had not had any contact with them.

Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent.

Many - particularly in eastern Europe - feel their security is linked to that of Ukraine. Agreements cannot be implemented "if no consensus can be reached among Nato members," a German government spokesperson said on Wednesday.

Kushner said the US was keen to bring the Europeans on board and said that getting them "added to the format" would be on the agenda for his talks with Putin.

There is also disagreement on whether discussions on a future security framework should be preceded by a ceasefire, as the Europeans and Kyiv would want, or whether the fighting only stops after an agreement has been reached, as the Kremlin has insisted.

Any agreement on a peacetime security framework, however, is contingent on the war ending, Kushner noted. But that cannot occur "until there's an agreement on territory and on all other bilateral issues," he added.

Since talks began last year, a core obstacle to any settlement has been Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is mostly occupied by Russia. Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those areas, which it says are essential to its security.

Moscow, meanwhile, has never backed down from its demand that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk it still holds. "Every inch" of land would be "returned to Russia one way or another", Medinsky said.

Kushner acknowledged that the territorial question remained the hardest, while Zelensky's chief of staff and negotiator Kyrylo Budanov refused to be drawn on whether Russia was still demanding a Ukrainian withdrawal from the region.

Later, Budanov admitted the talks had been "tough" and that Ukraine's priority was to ensure Russia could not attack it again.

"These deals are very hard and complex, and this one is very emotional, very complex," Kushner said. "The reality is there is no trust right now between the sides and that is to be expected after a conflict like this."

articles.summary: Iran refuses to surrender enriched uranium, threatens to strike US bases in Europe if attacked Submitted by MEE staff on Wed, 11/11/2026 - 16:40 Security chief Mohsen Rezaei warns Tehran will reciprocate against any US attack emanating from Europe Secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei attends consultations with members of the Mecca Joint Defence in Tehran, Iran, on 26 October 2026 (Iranian Presidency via Zuma Press) Off Iran has no intention of surrendering its enriched nuclear material, which it wants to use to build nuclear-powered submarines, security chief Mohsen Rezaei said on Wednesday, in an apparent rejection of US demands to give up the material for a political settlement. In an interview with Al Mayadeen TV network, Rezaei said Iran will not allow a “single speck” of enriched uranium to leave the country. "We need the enriched material to design ships and submarines that work on nuclear energy," Rezaei said, adding that Tehran has informed Moscow that its enriched nuclear material will remain in the country and "we will use it ourselves". Rezaei’s remarks come a day after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called Iran’s terms for a political settlement “absurd” and stressed that the Trump administration believes its maritime blockade against Iran gives them the upper hand in negotiations. Rezaei, who has become more prominent in the media in recent months for explaining Iran’s terms, struck a defiant tone in his interview. “If American aircraft take off from an American military base, even one located in a European country or some other distant region, to bomb Iran, we will strike those bases as well," Rezaei said. He also said that Iran's response to renewed US attacks would "target America's more distant military installations - including the ones we have not yet attacked", without specifying details. "We may even strike certain islands that they assume are beyond the reach of our missiles," he added. Rezaei may be referring to Diego Garcia , the Indian Ocean island where the US has access to a military base. The US is widely believed to have used the base in its February 2026 attack and in the following months. The Trump administration has used deescalatory language since the Republican Party was badly defeated in US midterm elections on 3 November by the Democrats, who campaigned against the war and rising energy prices. While US President Donald Trump has said that the war was “effectively over” and that there was “momentum” to end the conflict, the two sides seem far apart on files including nuclear enrichment, sanctions relief and control over the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian missile capabilities While the Trump administration has characterised Iran as a defeated foe, Tehran appears to be working to recover from the US-Israeli attacks that began in February. Bloomberg reported on Tuesday that Iran is now capable of building about 50 ballistic missiles per month, or roughly half its prewar capacity, providing a substantial arsenal should the US and Israel resume attacking. US says no need for new attacks but calls Iran's peace terms 'absurd' ed as a new underground "missile city", housing ballistic and cruise missiles, according to a report by Tasnim news agency. The US’s Gulf allies bore the brunt of Iran’s retaliation over the US-Israeli attack, with the UAE, Qatar, Bahrain, and Kuwait facing thousands of missile and drone strikes. While direct attacks have stopped, Iran is still striking vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, as it looks to compete with the US for control over the waterway. The Houthis, who are aligned with Iran, are also bombing Saudi Arabia, as they look to extend their territory in Yemen. On Wednesday, insurer Allianz Trade said Gulf countries face more than $200bn in damage and economic losses from the war, and the number could quadruple by 2030. "Physical damage across the region is assessed [at] just above $200bn, mostly concentrated in Hormuz-locked economies, especially in energy infrastructure," the insurer said in a report.
