articles.title: Tens of thousands join Poland’s nationalist Independence Day march
articles.summary: Polish PM Donald Tusk calls for restraint, urging unity after deadly Krakow attack linked to far-right ideology.
articles.preview: Polish PM Donald Tusk calls for restraint, urging unity after deadly Krakow attack linked to far-right ideology. Tens of thousands of nationalist sympathisers have gathered in Poland’s capital, Warsaw, for an Independence Day march, days after a mass shooting in Krakow killed six people. Participants carrying Polish flags assembled in central Warsaw on Wednesday, as police officers were deployed at the scene to secure the demonstration.
articles.body:
Polish PM Donald Tusk calls for restraint, urging unity after deadly Krakow attack linked to far-right ideology.

Tens of thousands of nationalist sympathisers have gathered in Poland’s capital, Warsaw, for an Independence Day march, days after a mass shooting in Krakow killed six people.

Participants carrying Polish flags assembled in central Warsaw on Wednesday, as police officers were deployed at the scene to secure the demonstration.

The Independence Day march, which has long been a source of tension between right-wing groups and Poland’s governing centrists, has been held annually on November 11 since 1918 to commemorate the end of more than 100 years of partition by Russia, Prussia and Austria.

The annual march has faced criticism for anti-Semitic and anti-immigration rhetoric, while supporters say the gathering, held under the motto “A Pole is the host in Poland”, is an expression of national pride.

Anticipated turnout

Organisers of the march said they expected a record turnout, with many foreign nationalists set to attend, including Spain’s Revuelta, a youth movement linked to Vox, and members of the Hungarian far-right Mi Hazank party.

Poland’s conservative-nationalist President Karol Nawrocki was seen attending the march and has previously participated in both his official capacity and as a private citizen.

Poland “does not exist today so that the political elites can grant themselves the right to manage citizens … against the will of the nation”, Nawrocki said, alluding to the centrist government.

Prior to the march, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk appealed for restraint amid heightened political divisions after ministers said the man who killed six people and wounded more than a dozen in the main square of Krakow on Saturday, November 7 may have been motivated by far-right ideology.

“We may hold different views, we may keep each other in check, and at times we may even be political opponents,” Tusk said. “Anyone who truly cares about Poland must understand that this space, defined by independence, freedom and a secure Republic, is a common good.”

On Tuesday, Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek said the killer had been interested in the neo-Nazi Anders Behring Breivik, who killed 77 people in Norway in 2011.

On Monday, the police announced that the 24-year-old gunman died at a hospital after he was shot by police officers and arrested on Saturday when he opened fire from his car.

articles.title: Iran's top negotiator says Tehran has no desire for war to continue
articles.summary: Iran's top negotiator says Tehran has no desire for war to continue Iran's parliament speaker and head of its negotiating team, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said in an interview with Al Jazeera on Wednesday that Tehran has no desire to continue the war with the US, but the ball is in Washington's court for peace talks. Ghalibaf said that Iran provided the US with a clear and transparent response outlining its demands, but the Trump administration has not yet reponded. An agreement with Washington is possible, he added, provided it adheres to what was previously agreed upon and refrains from actions that undermine trust and excessive demands. He said that Iran is determined to move beyond the state of “no war, no peace” through negotiations or sustainable deterrence, and accused Washington of imposing a siege on the country by blocking access to food and hindering trade and healthcare services. However, he said that the Strait of Hormuz will not return to its pre-war status, adding that its future would be determined within a seven-point framework proposed by Tehran. Finally, Ghalibaf told Al Jazeera that the US visited Moscow and asked President Vladimir Putin to speak with Iran to facilitate direct negotiations. Iran's Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf speaks to reporters in the central holy city of Najaf on 21 August 2026 (Qassem al-Kaabi/AFP)

articles.body:
Russia and Ukraine have agreed to the “largest prisoner exchange” of the war at their first US-brokered talks since February but made little progress towards a broader peace agreement.

Both sides sent senior delegations to the two-day talks, led by Donald Trump’s envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, in an effort to find a solution to end the nearly-five-year war.

David Arakhamia, a senior member of Ukraine’s delegation, said the Russian team had arrived with “very, very strict directives”, making it difficult to narrow differences. But he said there had been “really big progress” on security guarantees for Ukraine after the war. “I think we have good momentum to bring about a solution before the new year,” Arakhamia said.

Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, also struck an upbeat tone, saying he could see a path to an agreement. “These deals are very hard and complex, and this one is very emotional, very complex. It’s a very hot war,” he said. “But we see all the different ingredients to make a deal. We just have to figure out how to refine those ingredients, organise them and create the right structure and pathway.”

Kushner said the planned exchange, expected to involve more than 1,000 prisoners from each side, would “reunite families, build trust and create momentum towards peace”.

The US envoys are due to travel to Moscow on Thursday to discuss the Abu Dhabi talks with Vladimir Putin, before heading to Dublin, where they are expected to meet Volodymyr Zelenskyy and a group of European partners.

“In close coordination with Ukraine and our European partners, we have aligned on proposals we will discuss with President Putin in Moscow tomorrow, followed by consultations with President Zelenskyy,” Kushner said.

But despite the optimism, Kushner also said the two sides had yet to resolve their territorial dispute.

Russia’s territorial demands have shifted over time, but Moscow has made clear it wants control of all the Donbas, including areas still held by Kyiv, as well as the parts of two southern regions it does not yet occupy.

Vladimir Medinsky, the hardline Russian official who led Moscow’s delegation, said that “every inch of our land will be returned to Russia, one way or another,” in a sign that Moscow was unwilling to soften its territorial demands. Russia would be satisfied with the negotiations only “when there is peace on its terms”, he added.

He also said the main task was to create a new security system in Europe that would become “a new Yalta and Potsdam”.

Medinsky said Europe’s post-second world war security system was failing, with Ukraine merely the place where its wider problems had erupted. “Essentially, the whole body is sick, and Ukraine was just a cyst that burst. The whole body must be cured. A Band-Aid won’t be enough,” Medinsky said.

His focus on Europe’s wider security order is likely to heighten concern among European leaders that Washington and Moscow could reach a broader agreement on the continent’s security, potentially limiting Nato’s military presence in eastern Europe.

Russia appears to be seeking to revive demands it presented to Nato in 2021, including a halt to further enlargement that would rule out Ukraine’s membership, restrictions on Nato forces and weapons in European countries that joined after 1997, and limits on missile deployments.

That ultimatum was dismissed as a non-starter by the west and, weeks later, Russia invaded Ukraine.

Concerned that Europe’s security future could be discussed over their heads, European governments sent envoys to Abu Dhabi to try to influence the talks, although they are not believed to have taken part directly.

Medinsky dismissed their presence, saying that if they had come “as tourists”, they could talk in the hotel lobby, and that Russia would consider proposals only if they had “something specific” to offer.

European leaders have increasingly discussed the need for a direct channel to Putin, but no clear candidate has emerged. The leaders of Norway and Finland have recently spoken to the Russian president, while Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said on Wednesday that he was open to doing so.

Kushner, meanwhile, said Europe should choose a single representative to speak on its behalf. “If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiations,” he said.

He stressed that one of the aims of his trip to Moscow was to “see if we can get Europeans added” to future talks. “The issues that were covered in these discussions were really postwar security,” he said. “How do we make sure that once this war ends, it doesn’t start again?”

Russian officials have long opposed European participation, arguing that countries supplying weapons to Kyiv cannot act as impartial mediators. Medinsky said Russia would speak to European countries only “when their conscience awakens” and they stop supplying Ukraine with weapons.

As diplomatic efforts continued, both sides kept up their attacks. Russia launched drones at Kyiv and other regions during the day, while Ukraine struck the Ust-Luga port on Russia’s Baltic coast overnight. The port, in the Leningrad region, is a major route for Russian energy exports and was still burning on Wednesday.

articles.body:
Ukraine

Russian and Ukrainian negotiators said some progress was made in two days of peace talks in Abu Dhabi that ended on Wednesday.

They agreed to a large exchange of prisoners of war, but there was no major breakthrough on ending the conflict that began with Moscow’s full-scale invasion nearly five years ago.

Hopes had been low for any significant development in the first meeting in nine months between the delegations.

Russia and Ukraine have from time to time swapped POWs but have remained far apart in their demands for accepting a peace settlement.

United States envoy, Jared Kushner, described the talks as “very substantive” with “some pretty tough discussions” after the long pause.

“But obviously there's a lot of very serious issues that are being discussed, but the conversations were very thorough,” he said.

He said they covered all of the relevant issues and were able to “do a good exchange of ideas”.

“Some areas we see places where we can find compromises, others we need to have more discussions. But I think this was a good first step,” Kushner added.

Despite the positive note, US mediators say there is a lack of trust between the warring sides.

As well as postwar security guarantees for both countries, another key hurdle is the fate of Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory.

Kushner is due to meet with the presidents of both countries later this week. In talks with Russia’s Vladimir Putin, he is expected to raise the question of including European partners.

Representatives of European governments, the European Union, and NATO were in the United Arab Emirates capital, but did not attend the three-way discussions.

EU officials were excluded by Moscow from the talks.

Moscow doesn’t want European countries, which are concerned about Russia’s conduct and broader intentions on the continent, involved in the direct negotiations.

These latest talks were held in a new political atmosphere as the Trump administration now has to reckon with Democrats taking control of the US Congress in January.

They could demand more support for Ukraine.

The negotiations also come against the backdrop of continued fighting on the frontline, where little territory has changed hands this year.

Analysts and humanitarian organisations say the ongoing conflict has resulted in the death of hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians.

articles.summary: Lebanese wheat production hit by war as farmlands face severe destruction in the south and Bekaa Valley.

articles.body:
Lebanese wheat production hit by war as farmlands face severe destruction in the south and Bekaa Valley.

Israel’s war on Lebanon has damaged the country’s wheat production and harmed the lives of farmers, experts told Al Jazeera.

For the last three years, Israel has been waging a war on Lebanon, where it has occupied large parts of the south and destroyed homes and infrastructure, in what some experts have said is a deliberate effort to make the land uninhabitable.

Repeated Israeli attacks have created havoc on the country’s wheat production, particularly in the south and in eastern Lebanon’s Bekaa Valley, where lands abandoned due to the impacts of war have increased to around 24 percent.

“They’re disrupting entire ecosystems,” Munira Khayyat, author of A Landscape of War: Ecologies of Resistance and Survival in South Lebanon, told Al Jazeera. “[Israel is] advancing the possibilities of drought and desertification, basically weakening the capacity of this land to hold life.”

Farmlands damaged

Since 2023, Israel has been attacking large swaths of southern Lebanon, including using chemicals like white phosphorus, in what analysts and locals said was an effort to make the ground sterile or uninhabitable. A ceasefire was brokered in 2024 by France and the United States, but Israel never stopped attacking targets in Lebanon.

On March 2, Israel escalated its war on Lebanon for the second time in under two years. Hezbollah had attacked Israel following Israel’s assassination of Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei two days earlier. The group also said it was in response to near-daily ceasefire violations by Israel.

Since then, Israel has reinvaded southern Lebanon, taking land up to 10 kilometres (6.2 miles) inside the country. Beirut and Tel Aviv signed a US-brokered framework agreement in June, which was supposed to put into motion so-called “pilot zones”. Under these pilot zones, Israeli troops would withdraw to be replaced by the Lebanese Armed Forces, who would also work to disarm Hezbollah.

Instead, Israeli troops have continued to level destruction in southern Lebanon, detonating homes and crucial infrastructure, including farmland.

“The South [of Lebanon] experienced the highest average losses [in wheat-growing areas], reaching 47 percent in 2023-2024 and 61 percent in 2024-2025,” Mariam Ibrahim, a researcher with Lebanon’s National Council for Scientific Research [CNRS-L] and author of a recent paper called “Wheat in Crisis” that tracked Lebanon’s wheat struggles from 2017 to 2025, told Al Jazeera. “The Bekaa plain, which accounts for approximately 64 percent of Lebanon’s national wheat production, was also significantly affected, losing around 43 percent and 57 percent of its wheat area during the two respective seasons.”

In areas like the border town Bint Jbeil, 100 percent of cropland was destroyed, while in the Baalbeck district to the east, the study says approximately 32 percent of cropland was destroyed.

Wheat price influences

Ibrahim said the Russian-Ukrainian war led to an increase in bread prices and incentivised some domestic Lebanese production.

“The depreciation of the Lebanese pound meant that farmers could potentially generate higher revenues and profits in local currency when selling their wheat, as wheat prices were increasingly influenced by international market prices,” she said. “This provided an additional economic incentive to expand wheat cultivation, and our results showed that Lebanon’s wheat cultivation area reached its peak [during] the 2022-2023 season.”

However, experts said that since 2023, Israel’s war on Lebanon led to the proportion of land that had been used to grow wheat that was now left fallow increasing from 9 percent to 24 percent, mostly in the south and the Bekaa Valley.

Elias Ghadban, a food security expert with the independent Beirut-based consultancy firm AgriDev, told Al Jazeera that the destruction of land used to farm wheat has not made a “significant difference” at the national level, but it has had a damaging effect on southern wheat farmers who “lost their livelihoods”.

Ghadban also pointed to the fact that the cost of living has increased in Lebanon while salaries have failed to match that increase. “The expenditure on basic needs went up,” he said.

The economic crisis, followed by three years of war, has devastated many farmers, particularly as much of southern Lebanon’s farmland is largely unindustrialised. Experts warn that the destruction caused by Israel’s war could prevent many farmers from rebuilding their livelihoods, even after the fighting ends.

“All those small farmers who have made southern Lebanon what it is today and have been able to hold that land through their attachment to it, through their farming of it, through their existential need to be on that land in order to make their lives viable, that’s going to be broken,” Khayyat said.

articles.body:
“Is Maga dead?” asked Margaret, a Guardian reader in Switzerland, in a live Q&A with our correspondents after the seismic US midterm elections. If Margaret’s query expressed a hope that the Democrats’ blue wave could transform Europe’s fortunes after two years of Maga-induced trauma, she was probably not alone.

The resounding defeat for Donald Trump’s Republicans and the installation of a Democratic-controlled US Congress has been met with understandable relief in European capitals. In the short term however, the worst for Europe is not over. Trump didn’t need congressional approval, after all, to unleash a trade war on his supposed European allies, threaten to invade Greenland, try to stitch up Ukraine or go to war with Iran, an act that has inflated fuel and food prices disastrously.

Hemmed in now on domestic policy, the US president may, many European leaders fear, use his extensive foreign policy powers to become even more confrontational on the world stage. Europe, warned Nathalie Tocci, is exactly where Trump will lash out. “Trump and Maga have always seen Europe as the mirror image of their domestic foes: a bunch of presumptuous, woke, emasculated liberals. Now that those foes have made a comeback at home, Trump’s rancour towards Europe is likely to grow.”

The lashing out could come in the form of new tariff chaos. As the humiliated Maga figurehead (one Washington expert likened the movement now to “a cornered ferret”), Trump could veto aid for Ukraine and thwart Kyiv’s access to defence technology. Paul Taylor sketched a fearful scenario in which he could even attempt a carve-up of eastern Europe in the so-called “big, beautiful deal” for Ukraine that he says he is working on with Russia. The omens for Europe were poor as US-mediated talks opened in Abu Dhabi, with delegates from Germany, France, the UK and the EU, literally sidelined.

Nor can Europe rely on the new intake of congressional Democrats to challenge Trump on its behalf, Blanche Leridon of the Institut Montaigne thinktank in Paris, tells me. “We have to be clear-sighted that the Democrats’ priority in Congress won’t be to re-establish a more harmonious relationship with Europe. Their foreign policy is, at this point, difficult to decipher. There isn’t a single, consistent position between the more progressive and centrist factions when it comes to either Europe or Ukraine specifically.”

We can’t even assume that nationalist populist parties, encouraged by Trump to destroy the EU from the inside, will suffer by their association with him. True, in central and eastern Europe, where the Maga spirit was heavily promoted by Viktor Orbán, some incumbents may have to perform a pivot. Poland’s conservative president Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by the opposition Eurosceptic Law and Justice party and has vaunted his proximity to Trump, is now facing awkward questions. And in Czechia, which has one of the most pro-Maga governments in Europe, populist PM Andrej Babiš and his far-right coalition partners, the Motorists party, have faced a wave of grassroots protests lately.

In Italy meanwhile, the far-right prime minister Giorgia Meloni played up tensions with Trump months ago, a strategic move to allay the concerns of voters, the majority of whom despise him.

But in countries where populists have not yet been in government and are polling at record levels, Trump’s humiliation may not matter to voters, even if their grievances – such as stagnant pay, inflation and lack of affordable housing – are often driven by global forces.

“It would be wrong to conclude that national-populist and reactionary forces are in retreat everywhere in the west,” Leridon says. “The Democrats won in the US because people were fed up with Trump, in Serbia, [Aleksandar] Vučić was overthrown after 14 years, but in countries where populist political forces are not in power, but on the verge of gaining it, the calculation is different.”

In France, Marine Le Pen is still leading in the polls, six months ahead of a presidential election being fought on cost-of-living issues. Her far-right National Rally party identified Trump as a liability some time ago. “Le Pen and [Jordan] Bardella understood perfectly the radioactive effect the US president could have on them as politicians claiming to defend French national interests. Above all, they recoiled from the corrosive impact of Trump’s policies on purchasing power in France, whether via trade tariffs or the war in Iran,” Leridon says.

In Germany, Alice Weidel, a co-leader of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland, had also distanced the party from Trump in response to tariffs and Greenland. Weidel now blames Trump’s defeat on broken promises about going to war with Iran.

A critical test for Europe’s political direction is looming in Spain. Socialist prime minister Pedro Sánchez, who called a snap election for 29 November, welcomed Trump’s defeat as a straw in the wind for the revival of progressive forces. But amid public outcry over housing and wages (the cause of Wednesday’s general strike), the momentum is with the opposition rightwing Popular Party (PP) – which could coalesce with the far-right Vox. If this happens, it will be the first time a far-right party enters government in Spain since the end of the Franco dictatorship in 1975. Santiago Abascal, the Vox leader, dismissed any suggestion of an ideological connection with Trump’s Republicans. “We are in Spain, not in Michigan,” he said after the midterms.

A yearning for generational change

And yet, longer term, the broader, more hopeful lesson from across the Atlantic could be that after years of global backsliding liberal democracy is not dead. “If Europe can celebrate an essential point, it is that American democracy is alive and was the big winner of these elections,” Leridon says.

Could this even, as Alexander Hurst asked, be a “democratic spring” – one that began in Budapest in April with Orbán’s defeat? Julian Borger unpacked how a sequence of four pivotal elections this year, in Hungary, Serbia, Brazil and now the US, has shown the power of grassroots activism to produce surprises and could, perhaps, begin the reversal of a worldwide drift towards authoritarianism.

The US vote could even shake Europe’s ailing mainstream parties out of their fatalistic mimicking of far-right policies and into action. Gen Z voters fuelled the US blue wave, which showed a yearning for generational change. At a time when youth-led protest movements have rocked Europe, progressive parties may be able to channel protest energy into serious political change. They can’t say they haven’t been warned, loudly, to heed calls for democratic renewal, education, decent housing, equality and limits on the power of the big tech billionaires. Or that failure to do so could allow grassroots anger to be co-opted into the same kind of anti-system nihilism that fuelled Maga.

articles.title: Can Tehran survive a ‘zero oil’ budget, if US blockade on Iran persists?
articles.summary: The government is defiant and planning for the worst, but a US siege is expected to make most Iranians poorer.
articles.preview: The government is defiant and planning for the worst, but persisting siege is expected to make most Iranians poorer over the coming months. Tehran, Iran – After months of oscillating between new bouts of fighting and negotiations, the administration of United States President Donald Trump has reportedly opted for a third option – gradual economic pressure on Tehran.
articles.body:
The government is defiant and planning for the worst, but persisting siege is expected to make most Iranians poorer over the coming months.

Tehran, Iran – After months of oscillating between new bouts of fighting and negotiations, the administration of United States President Donald Trump has reportedly opted for a third option – gradual economic pressure on Tehran.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told his Group of Seven (G7) counterparts in Paris on Tuesday that a naval blockade, stringent sanctions and overland border disruptions could continue without a clear endpoint in sight, according to US media. He later said that Iran’s economy “continues to collapse” and predicted worsening conditions over the next one to three months.

Tehran-based economist and market analyst Isaac Saidian said that if the persistent economic siege on Iran brings the country’s oil incomes down to near-zero levels, Tehran will be faced with one of the most difficult challenges in its recent history.

“The issue is not just a decline in foreign currency incomes, but the government’s ability to account for current expenditure, paying salaries and pensions, providing essential goods, preserving the value of the national currency, and preventing budget deficits from turning into a new inflationary wave,” Saidian told Al Jazeera.

Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian has indicated that the cash-strapped civilian government is preparing to deal with a prolonged economic crisis caused by siege and sanctions, but has admitted that the lingering “no war, no peace” conditions will be harmful.

But the authorities have stressed that there are no prospects of economic collapse. They have also raised the prospect of “breaking the blockade” if necessary, although it remains unclear by what means.

In a budget directive on November 3, Pezeshkian’s administration set out two scenarios. One was the continuation of sanctions, the maritime blockade and present regional conditions. The other prediction was an improvement of the situation involving fewer financial and commercial restrictions, including a substantial or complete removal of the blockade.

“The government must prepare for circumstances in which oil revenue reaches zero,” Mohammad Ghasemi, deputy for coordination of planning and budget at Iran’s Plan and Budget Organization, told local media on Monday about a contingency for next year.

The US military first imposed a naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports, through which most of the country’s trade passed, on April 13. A memorandum of understanding in June lifted the blockade and allowed some oil and trade to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, but the deal fell apart within weeks. The second blockade has been in place since July 14, as Iran and the US fight for control of the Strait of Hormuz.

The US military says it has redirected 147 ships and disabled five while enforcing the blockade. It also claimed to have destroyed 10 Iranian oil tankers linked to the shadow fleet of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). According to the US Treasury, the blockade has led to Iran loading no oil onto vessels since August 25.

A late October assessment by Kpler said Iran’s oil production had fallen below 2 million barrels a day in the preceding months. Iran produced 3.45 million barrels of crude per day in January and 3.59 million in the following month, but Israel and the US’s war on Iran began on February 28.

The volume of Iranian crude and condensate floating outside the blockade zone had also fallen from 88.8 million barrels on July 14 to zero in mid-October. Because Chinese buyers generally pay one to two months after discharge, Kpler anticipated crude and condensate receipts potentially drying up around mid-December. Around 43 million barrels remain stranded inside the blockade area.

The US sanctions have also limited air travel to and from Iran, while a new US task force announced this week aims at closing or disrupting most of Iran’s land borders with its seven neighbours.

The Iranian economy has already been dealing with chronic inflation, falling investments and purchasing power, as well as banking and budget imbalances for years. So removing oil revenues will undoubtedly exacerbate the situation.

The government has increasingly relied on taxes to account for a larger share of the budget, but oil still accounted for roughly one-third of planned government funding in the 2026–27 budget proposal.

Economist Saidian said if oil revenues fall sharply, the government’s next step should be to review public spending. Cutting spending on overlapping administrative structures and opaque budgetary grants, while suspending low-return public investment projects, could ease some of the fiscal pressure on the state, he said.

Reforming tax exemptions and tackling tax evasion, as well as carefully managed bond issuance and sale of some non-essential government assets, are other options. But he cautioned that any abrupt drops in salaries, pensions, or social support budgets would only deepen poverty.

The government has signalled that it will likely have to resort to reducing fuel and other energy subsidies again, which will increase prices, but the process will be gradual to lessen the impact on inflation.

“Expanding non-oil exports and facilitating trade with neighbouring countries are also essential,” Saidian said. “Even so, these exports cannot be expected to replace oil revenue in the short term, especially while restrictions on banking, insurance and transport remain in place.”

Government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani said on Tuesday that next year’s budget would prioritise inflation control through fiscal discipline, household support and tighter oversight of banks. The administration will continue handing out electronic food coupons, although it has been struggling to preserve their value due to runaway prices.

Year-on-year inflation was at nearly 89 percent in the Iranian calendar month ending October 22, according to the Statistical Center of Iran.

Saidian pointed out that no amount of austerity measures or budget reforms can fully replace sustainable access to foreign trade, investment and foreign currency incomes, so exiting inflationary stagnation for a prolonged period would require reduced tensions.

“The historical significance of the 2027-28 budget lies in what it can reveal about how prepared Iran’s government is to move beyond an oil-dependent economy and toward transparent, accountable fiscal governance. The budget should not merely be a plan to manage the government in a difficult year, but a plan to prevent passing on today’s crisis to future generations and to start structural reforms in Iran’s economy,” he said.

“The greatest danger is not that the government might run short of funds for a few months. The real danger is that it could stay afloat on paper while passing the cost of doing so on to the public, leaving society poorer, eroding the middle class, widening poverty and weakening the country’s productive capacity.”

articles.summary: I numeri sono in aumento e negli ultimi anni sono state introdotte nuove regole e stanziate risorse per prevenire e contrastare le minacce. Ma capire quanto queste misure abbiano funzionato non è semplice

articles.body:
L’allarme bomba scattato l’11 novembre in decine di scuole italiane, dopo l’invio di una mail anonima che ha segnalato la presenza di ordigni esplosivi negli edifici, è solo l’ultimo episodio di una serie di minacce che negli ultimi giorni ha interessato il nostro Paese. Nei giorni precedenti, messaggi analoghi erano stati inviati a diversi aeroporti, provocando controlli su alcuni voli e modifiche su alcune rotte.

Questi episodi si inseriscono in un quadro che ha riportato l’attenzione sulle minacce informatiche e la capacità dell’Italia di contrastarle efficacemente. Il 7 novembre il ministero degli Esteri aveva reso nota la diffusione sul dark web di dati personali del ministro Antonio Tajani. Il Ministro ha collegato le minacce alla posizione italiana sulla guerra in Ucraina e ha chiesto di affrontare il tema delle minacce ibride al G7 degli Esteri, che si è svolto a Parigi il 9 e 10 novembre. Un altro episodio era stato registrato a inizio novembre, quando alcuni supermercati italiani erano stati colpiti da attacchi informatici ai sistemi di refrigerazione, sui cui il governo aveva fatto il punto in una riunione il 3 novembre,

Il 9 novembre il ministro della Difesa Guido Crosetto, in un’intervista al Corriere della Sera, ha definito la guerra ibrida una «sfida epocale», che deve essere affrontata tramite una strategia comune tra le istituzioni. Una posizione in linea con quanto detto qualche giorno dalla presidente del Consiglio Giorgia Meloni, che aveva richiamato l’attenzione sui possibili effetti degli attacchi informatici, sottolineando i rischi per le infrastrutture civili.

Negli ultimi anni, l’Italia ha introdotto nuove regole, istituito strutture dedicate alla cybersicurezza e stanziato risorse per proteggere le proprie infrastrutture digitali. Ma quali interventi sono stati realizzati e che cosa dicono i dati disponibili sulla loro efficacia?

articles.body:
The US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, has relocated from his home in the Washington area to a military base after an Iranian threat against his life, the New York Times has reported.

Bessent has spearheaded a US push to cripple Iran’s economy since the start of the Middle East war, vowing “economic asphyxiation” of the Islamic republic through a web of sanctions.

He is one of a number of senior figures in the Trump administration including the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, and the new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, to leave their home to live on a military base or protected housing.

The US national intelligence chief, Jay Clayton, said last month that Tehran had “substantially increased” its efforts to target Americans in the Middle East and beyond.

These include intensifying the targeting of current and former US officials such as Bessent, the NYT reported on Tuesday, citing three sources familiar with the matter.

Iranian plotting against US officials has reached a “more advanced stage”, according to the anonymous sources, but the severity of the threats against Bessent was unclear.

Washington ordered non-essential US embassy staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia last month, after increasing attacks from Tehran-backed Houthi fighters.

The US military has also removed some aircraft from two British bases in recent weeks amid reported threats from Iran.

Diplomatic efforts to end the war are gathering pace, with Rubio saying on Tuesday that the US squeezing of Iran’s economy had made further attacks unnecessary.

Bessent has led the US sanctions and economic pressure campaign against Iran, called Operation Economic Outcast, since August to try to push Tehran to end attacks on shipping and reopen the strait of Hormuz. The crucial waterway has been largely closed since the US and Israel attacked Iran on 28 February.

The economic pressure campaign, which coincides with a US naval blockade of Iranian ports, has included sanctions on Middle Eastern bank branches and other financial services firms facilitating transactions with Iran.

A US Treasury spokesperson said: “The secretary will not be deterred by the Iranian regime’s threats and remains committed to executing Operation Economic Outcast and maintaining the blockade, which together are collapsing Iran’s economy.”

The Times reported that the severity of the threats to Bessent was not immediately clear.

A source familiar with the matter said security concerns surrounding Bessent had increased when the Wall Street Journal published an aerial view of the Georgetown mansion that Bessent bought for $12.5m (£9.4m) shortly after his confirmation as Treasury secretary in January 2025.

The photo allowed Bessent’s home to be geolocated, and Bessent was relocated to a military base for his safety, the source said, adding: “The news media has an obligation to act responsibly amid growing threats against public officials.”

Iran has previously denied plotting to attack officials and people on US soil.

Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed to this report

A western intelligence estimate says Iran can build about 50 ballistic missiles per month — roughly half its prewar capacity — providing a formidable means of retaliation if hostilities resume, despite months of airstrikes.

articles.title: Prove di forza tra il congresso statunitense e la Casa Bianca

articles.body:
Il segretario alla guerra statunitense Pete Hegseth sarà il primo capro espiatorio del trumpismo sconfitto? Nella notte è sopravvissuto a un tentativo di destituzione, ma per il ministro più criticato dell’amministrazione i problemi non sono finiti.

La procedura per la sua messa in stato d’accusa era stata avviata da un parlamentare repubblicano, non da un democratico. Thomas Massie, eletto in Kentucky alla camera dei rappresentanti, ha i suoi motivi per avercela con Hegseth. Per essersi opposto alla guerra contro l’Iran, Massie è stato preso di mira da Donald Trump, che gli ha fatto perdere le primarie repubblicane a beneficio di un candidato più leale. Massie, dunque, non farà parte del prossimo congresso statunitense.

Il suo atteggiamento “ribelle” spiega perché i repubblicani, che hanno la maggioranza nel congresso uscente e rimarranno in carica fino a gennaio, hanno fatto quadrato per evitare l’affronto a Hegseth. Trump è intervenuto personalmente per chiedere ai repubblicani di bloccare la procedura. Ma i democratici hanno tutta l’intenzione, da gennaio, di attaccare questo ministro così trumpiano da sembrare una caricatura.

Pete Hegseth è accusato di aver scatenato illegalmente la guerra contro l’Iran ignorando il parere del congresso e di aver compiuto atti di guerra, anch’essi illegali, contro alcune imbarcazioni nel mar dei Caraibi e contro il capo di un paese straniero, il venezuelano Nicolás Maduro. In sostanza, di aver violato la costituzione.

Fin dal suo ingresso nel governo è stato bersaglio di attacchi. I commentatori politici ritenevano che nel complesso Trump fosse tornato al potere più preparato della prima volta, ma la nomina di Hegseth è subito apparsa come una nota stonata.

Ex presentatore dell’emittente populista Fox News ed ex soldato in Afganistan e Iraq, Hegseth sembrava del tutto inadeguato a gestire un bilancio da mille miliardi di dollari e l’esercito più potente del mondo.

Ha fatto grandi epurazioni all’interno della gerarchia militare e ha moltiplicato le dichiarazioni polemiche contro la diversità (definendola un concetto “marxista”), contro i militari transgender e contro le donne, sostenendo che il testosterone sia un fattore di preparazione militare.

Hegseth è stato la persona dell’amministrazione più fedele a Donald Trump, un’aggravante per i suoi accusatori. Secondo il resoconto del New York Times, in occasione della riunione segreta alla Casa Bianca con Benjamin Netanyahu, Hegseth aveva sostenuto incondizionatamente la decisione del presidente di scatenare una guerra contro l’Iran.

Marco Rubio aveva definito bullshit (una stronzata) il piano israeliano, mentre il vicepresidente J.D. Vance continua a ripetere che era contrario. Solo Hegseth si era mostrato entusiasta.

Il giudizio più severo su di lui è arrivato da Nancy Lacore, ex viceammiraglia della flotta statunitense rimossa dall’incarico da Hegseth ed eletta la settimana scorsa al congresso: “Pete Hegseth è il ministro meno qualificato che questo paese abbia mai avuto”.

Se a gennaio gli attacchi riprenderanno in un congresso a maggioranza democratica, Trump dovrà chiedersi se valga la pena battersi per salvare Hegseth o se sacrificarlo per proteggere la presidenza nei prossimi due anni. Questa prima schermaglia dà un’idea di quello che verrà.

(Traduzione di Andrea Sparacino)

articles.title: The economic toll of Israel’s wars
articles.summary: Since the First Intifada in 1987, every major flare-up of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict has triggered a recession.
articles.preview: JERUSALEM – Israel’s election results make weeks of political negotiation all but certain. What is equally clear is that whatever government eventually takes office will need to begin reckoning with the mounting costs of Israel’s ongoing wars. Although Israel has been at war since October 2023, many observers argue that its economy has held up remarkably well, pointing to the booming stock market and the strength of the shekel as evidence. Has it? The answer depends on how we measure the economic costs of war.
articles.body:
JERUSALEM – Israel’s election results make weeks of political negotiation all but certain. What is equally clear is that whatever government eventually takes office will need to begin reckoning with the mounting costs of Israel’s ongoing wars.

Although Israel has been at war since October 2023, many observers argue that its economy has held up remarkably well, pointing to the booming stock market and the strength of the shekel as evidence. Has it?

The answer depends on how we measure the economic costs of war. Direct budgetary costs are measured primarily by the increase in defense expenditures. But then there are indirect costs, reflected in the impact on the business cycle, and the precedents are clear: Since the First Intifada in 1987, every major flare-up of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict has triggered a recession.

articles.body:
World News

Three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States opened Tuesday in the United Arab Emirates, as Washington renews its push to end the war that followed Moscow's all-out invasion nearly five years ago.

The two-day session in the UAE's capital, Abu Dhabi, is the first such meeting since February. It will focus on security guarantees, the White House said before the discussions. Russia sees NATO as a threat, and Ukraine wants to prevent future Russian invasions.

Hopes of progress in ending Europe’s biggest conflict since World War II are tempered by the absence of any significant breakthroughs in three previous rounds of talks early this year. The war has already killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians, analysts and humanitarian organizations say.

There are no signs the fighting is abating, and the talks took place against a backdrop of new long-range strikes between Russia and Ukraine. The two armies are largely deadlocked on the front line.

Russia launched 162 drones of various types and a ballistic missile at Ukraine overnight, Ukraine’s air force said.

Meanwhile, Russia’s Ministry of Defense said that its forces shot down 155 Ukrainian drones overnight above eight Russian regions, as well as the Crimean Peninsula, which Russia annexed from Ukraine in 2014.

articles.title: Gli Stati Uniti sbilanciano le trattative tra russi e ucraini
articles.summary: I rappresentati dei due paesi in guerra sono ad Abu Dhabi per il primo incontro formale da febbraio dell’anno scorso. Ma l’accondiscendenza di Trump verso Putin non fa ben sperare
articles.preview: Il 10 novembre russi e ucraini si ritrovano faccia a faccia ad Abu Dhabi, negli Emirati Arabi Uniti, per il primo incontro formale da febbraio dell’anno scorso. Insieme a loro ci sono Steve Witkoff e Jared Kushner, gli inviati di Donald Trump. Gli europei sono stati consultati, ma resteranno comunque esclusi dal dialogo. Ancora una volta emerge il solito interrogativo: è possibile fermare questa guerra che dura da quasi cinque anni e ha provocato un’ecatombe?
articles.body:
Il 10 novembre russi e ucraini si ritrovano faccia a faccia ad Abu Dhabi, negli Emirati Arabi Uniti, per il primo incontro formale da febbraio dell’anno scorso. Insieme a loro ci sono Steve Witkoff e Jared Kushner, gli inviati di Donald Trump. Gli europei sono stati consultati, ma resteranno comunque esclusi dal dialogo.

Ancora una volta emerge il solito interrogativo: è possibile fermare questa guerra che dura da quasi cinque anni e ha provocato un’ecatombe? Secondo i dati dell’istituto di statistica russo, rubati e diffusi da un gruppo di hacker, i morti sul fronte russo sarebbero 400mila, mentre le ultime stime parlano di 100mila vittime ucraine. Per non dire delle sofferenze di un popolo intero, che si appresta a trascorrere l’inverno più duro dall’inizio del conflitto.

Gli unici a volere un accordo a tutti i costi sono gli inviati di Trump. Il presidente statunitense, infatti, ha subìto una sconfitta elettorale umiliante e ha bisogno di cancellare l’immagine di loser, perdente. Il problema è che Trump appare del tutto accondiscendente nei confronti del presidente russo Vladimir Putin, come dimostra il fatto che alla vigilia dell’incontro abbia continuato ad attaccare quello ucraino, Volodymyr Zelenskyj, accusandolo di “mancanza di rispetto” nei confronti della Russia, senza criticare minimamente i bombardamenti dell’esercito russo contro obiettivi civili.

Tutto questo non lascia certo presagire una soluzione rapida, tanto più che Putin sembra convinto di poter piegare durante l’inverno la resistenza ucraina, approfittando delle difficoltà della difesa aerea del nemico e dei danni inflitti alle infrastrutture civili. Quasi ogni giorno la Russia compie azioni che costituirebbero crimini di guerra se solo il diritto internazionale umanitario fosse minimamente rispettato. Putin, però, può contare sulla debolezza degli europei e sulla certezza che Trump chiuderà un occhio.

Il presidente russo è sicuramente entusiasta davanti allo spettacolo delle divisioni europee, a cominciare dai sondaggi francesi che indicano come favoriti per il secondo turno due candidati che, ognuno a modo suo, indebolirebbero il sostegno all’Ucraina. Marine Le Pen ha dichiarato che la Francia “non ha più i mezzi” per assistere Kiev, mentre Jean-Luc Mélenchon propone un referendum nelle zone del Donbass controllate dall’esercito russo.

Il 9 novembre Kiev ha risposto al candidato della France insoumise ricordando il referendum del 1991 con cui l’83 per cento degli abitanti del Donbass votò per l’indipendenza, aggiungendo che “i referendum sotto occupazione sono uno strumento di annessione, non un’espressione della volontà popolare. Nessun paese civile e democratico accetterebbe questo processo per stabilire i suoi confini”.

L’Ucraina può sperare che la presenza degli europei ad Abu Dhabi, anche se nell’anticamera degli incontri e non al tavolo dei negoziati, possa scongiurare un tradimento troppo clamoroso. Di recente i rappresentanti del continente sono rimasti sconvolti quando hanno scoperto (all’ultimo minuto) che Trump aveva deciso di cancellare le sanzioni contro la Russia nel tentativo, poi risultato inutile, di far abbassare il prezzo del petrolio e limitare le perdite alle elezioni di metà mandato.

Per gli ucraini il nuovo parlamento statunitense, che si insedierà all’inizio di gennaio, è una buona notizia, perché vigilerà sull’applicazione delle sanzioni adottate in primavera su iniziativa del senatore repubblicano Lindsey Graham, morto poco dopo. Di sicuro il nuovo congresso sarà meno incline a favorire Putin.

Intanto il teatro pseudodiplomatico si sposta ad Abu Dhabi. Tuttavia, il tentativo di relegare la guerra in Ucraina all’ombra di un’altra guerra, quella in Iran, che Trump non riesce a risolvere, non lascia molto spazio all’ottimismo.

(Traduzione di Andrea Sparacino)

articles.title: Anthropic da el pistoletazo de salida a su OPV para minoristas en España
articles.summary: Los particulares nacionales pueden pedir acciones desde este miércoles a través de JP Morgan, Deutsche Bank, eToro, Interactive Brokers, flatexDEGIRO, Revolut, Trade Republic y Scalable Capital. El debut se celebrará en el Nasdaq el 19 de noviembre
articles.preview: Los particulares nacionales pueden pedir acciones desde este miércoles a través de JP Morgan, Deutsche Bank, eToro, Interactive Brokers, flatexDEGIRO, Revolut, Trade Republic y Scalable Capital. El debut se celebrará en el Nasdaq el 19 de noviembre Los pequeños inversores españoles ya tienen todas las instrucciones para entrar en Anthropic a través de su Oferta Pública de Venta (OPV) y Suscripción (OPS).
articles.body:
Los particulares nacionales pueden pedir acciones desde este miércoles a través de JP Morgan, Deutsche Bank, eToro, Interactive Brokers, flatexDEGIRO, Revolut, Trade Republic y Scalable Capital. El debut se celebrará en el Nasdaq el 19 de noviembre

Los pequeños inversores españoles ya tienen todas las instrucciones para entrar en Anthropic a través de su Oferta Pública de Venta (OPV) y Suscripción (OPS). El supervisor alemán, la BaFin, ha aprobado este miércoles el folleto europeo de la salida a Bolsa del laboratorio de inteligencia artificial y así podrá venderse ya en España, al igual que en otros países europeos. Los particulares españoles pueden solicitar acciones en JP Morgan y Deutsche Bank, así como en eToro, Interactive Brokers, flatexDEGIRO, Revolut, Trade Republic y Scalable Capital. El estreno en el Nasdaq está previsto para el 19 de noviembre. No hay importe mínimo en las órdenes, que se podrán cursar hasta el día anterior al del debut.

El tramo minorista se abre desde Wall Street a Alemania, Dinamarca, España, Finlandia, Francia, Irlanda, Noruega, Países Bajos, Suecia y Suiza. Como publicó CincoDías, ninguna entidad española participa en la colocación. En la OPV de SpaceX, el Santander coordinó el tramo minorista en España y los clientes de Renta 4 y GVC Gaesco pudieron acudir. Esta es la segunda colocación en Bolsa de este año que permite a los inversores españoles participar en su estreno, y la primera fue también originaria de Wall Street: SpaceX. Las últimas salidas a Bolsa en el parqué nacional con tramo para particulares fueron las de Aena, en 2015, y Opdenergy, en 2022.

En Europa, Antrophic venderá unos 80 millones de títulos, que, al precio medio del rango fijado en Estados Unidos de 74 dólares, suman unos 6.000 millones de dólares (5.300 millones de euros). Es casi la mitad de lo que Anthropic quiere reservar a los pequeños ahorradores de todo el mundo. Según el folleto registrado ante la Comisión de Bolsa y Valores de EE UU (SEC, por sus siglas en inglés), los minoristas de Estados Unidos y del resto de países pueden quedarse con hasta el 20% de la oferta. Respecto a los 825 millones de acciones, son unos 165 millones de títulos, por unos 12.000 millones de dólares (11.000 millones de euros) al precio medio. El resto, cerca de 85 millones de acciones, se repartirá entre los minoristas de Estados Unidos y de los otros cuatro países con OPV para minoristas: Reino Unido, Australia, Japón y Canadá.

En Estados Unidos, el folleto fija un rango orientativo de entre 70 y 78 dólares por acción (entre 62,4 y 69,5 euros), pero en Europa fija un precio máximo de 120 dólares (107 euros). Es un techo exigido por el reglamento europeo de folletos y que permite a Anthropic subir el rango si la demanda se dispara. Los coordinadores, Morgan Stanley y Goldman Sachs, y el resto de los bancos del sindicato abogan por un incremento del precio final, a tenor de la fuerte demanda, de varias veces el importe de la oferta (es decir, implica más de tres veces la cantidad ofertada). En todo caso, habrá un único precio para todos los inversores.

La operación es la mayor de la historia. Anthropic saca al mercado 825 millones de acciones, con 800 millones para la OPS y los casi 25 millones restantes para la OPV. Los bancos tienen además la opción de ampliar la operación (green shoe, en el argot) en otros 124 millones de títulos de nueva emisión. A esto se suma una colocación privada de 26.000 millones de dólares en acciones sin voto que suscribirán AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia y TSMC. En total, hasta 90.400 millones de dólares (80.600 millones de euros). Es decir, casi el 97% de la oferta base es ampliación de capital, de manera que, más que una OPV, es una OPS. La compañía aspira a una valoración de unos 1,4 billones de dólares, por debajo de lo que se manejaba hace un mes.

La pega está en el reparto. La oferta ha recibido ya varias veces más peticiones que acciones disponibles, según publicó este miércoles Bloomberg, impulsada por grandes órdenes de inversores ancla. El folleto avisa de que nadie tiene derecho a recibir todo lo que pide y de que cada intermediario adjudica con sus propios criterios. En SpaceX, Renta 4 dio prioridad a los primeros 10.000 euros de cada orden y ni siquiera llegó a cubrirlos. La demanda tampoco depende solo del entusiasmo. Anthropic redujo pérdidas y disparó sus ingresos en el tercer trimestre, y en la última versión del folleto, presentada el martes, elevó su facturación anualizada a 81.000 millones de dólares. Pedir acciones no garantiza recibirlas.

articles.title: OpenAI’s quarterly revenue reportedly crosses $10B for the first time
articles.summary: Sales of $10 billion represents an almost 50% jump from revenue of $6.7 billion the company recorded in the second quarter.
articles.preview: OpenAI is bouncing back from the doldrums it experienced earlier this year. The company’s quarterly revenue crossed $10 billion for the first time, thanks to strong demand for its recent AI models, Bloomberg reported, citing anonymous sources. If true, that would represent an almost 50% jump from the $6.7 billion in sales the company reportedly recorded in the second quarter. That would also mark a sizable increase in its revenue growth rate, which was previously said to be about 18% between the first and second quarters of the year.
articles.body:
OpenAI is bouncing back from the doldrums it experienced earlier this year. The company’s quarterly revenue crossed $10 billion for the first time, thanks to strong demand for its recent AI models, Bloomberg reported, citing anonymous sources.

If true, that would represent an almost 50% jump from the $6.7 billion in sales the company reportedly recorded in the second quarter. That would also mark a sizable increase in its revenue growth rate, which was previously said to be about 18% between the first and second quarters of the year.

OpenAI’s profitability picture also appears to have improved, with its adjusted operating margin narrowing from -150% in the second quarter to -109% in the third quarter, the report said.

OpenAI, one of the first to commercialize AI models, wasn’t exactly struggling to continue growing its top-line expansion — 18% growth on top of $5.7 billion in quarterly revenue is massive by any measure, especially compared to most software businesses.

But it was seeing those gains be trumped by its archrival Anthropic, which has taken the lead in capturing the enterprise market for AI models and recently reported Q3 revenue of $17 billion. OpenAI’s broader focus helped it attract a large user base and gain popularity early on, and it says it has over a billion users, but it’s reasonable to assume most of those are free users or subscribers to its cheapest plans.

Still, the company lagged Anthropic in catering to enterprises, a market where the Claude maker has pulled ahead, at least in terms of revenue growth.

OpenAI has recently benefited from a combination of tighter pricing, discounts, improving models, and a greater focus on building more enterprise-focused products and AI agents that can help people complete tasks.

OpenAI has now reached an annual revenue run rate of $50 billion, according to Bloomberg. Meanwhile, Anthropic, which is seeking a $1.4 trillion valuation in an IPO likely to happen soon, said yesterday that its annual revenue run rate had increased by $10 billion within a month to $81 billion as of the end of October.

(Note that OpenAI and Anthropic calculate their annualized revenue differently: Anthropic counts sales made by its cloud partners, while OpenAI only reports its share of some sales through its partners.)

None of those figures are small, of course, but the companies are also competing with models from Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google, as well as a plethora of cheaper but still highly capable models from open source AI labs, especially those from China.
